editorials.title: Dangerous phase: On the crisis in West Asia
editorials.passage:
The crisis in West Asia is escalating on two fronts. On Tuesday, the U.S. said that its forces had struck five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf waters after what it claimed were Tehran’s attacks on U.S. warships in the region. Iran retaliated with a massive ballistic missile attack on the Muwaffaq Salti U.S. air base in Jordan and vowed to respond with greater force to every U.S. attack from now on. It has also announced a new restricted zone in the Strait of Hormuz, warning commercial ships against crossing it under American naval escort. Separately, Yemen’s Houthis, who are closely aligned with Tehran, launched an attack on Saudi Arabia, wounding dozens. Riyadh has vowed a response. The Houthis, who control northern Yemen and parts of its Red Sea coast, have already enforced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia’s western ports and launched an offensive against the forces of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government in Taiz and Mocha. With both the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, and the Red Sea, a critical trade channel between Europe and Asia, remaining flashpoints, a horizontally escalating conflict from Tehran to Jordan and Riyadh to Bab-el Mandeb threatens to plunge the entire region into an economic and security abyss.

The current phase of the conflict could prove to be deadlier for several reasons. The U.S., which in the recent past has used intense military strikes and economic strangulation as separate policy tools in an attempt to force Iran to surrender, is now using both simultaneously to exert maximum pressure on Tehran. The U.S. naval blockade has largely prevented Iran from exporting its oil, while the American naval escort to a limited number of ships out of the Strait of Hormuz has helped Washington blunt the impact of Iran’s chokehold on the waterway on global energy prices. But President Donald Trump was wrong if he thought his maximum economic and military pressure would force Iran to make concessions. Iran, instead, decided to escalate the conflict by attacking American warships outside the Persian Gulf, fully aware that this would invite a stronger U.S. military response. Iran appears to believe that it has a window of opportunity with the U.S. heading into its midterm elections within weeks and Mr. Trump remaining politically weak at home. If Iran’s strikes on U.S. military vessels signal a clear decision at the top to escalate the conflict, its missile attack on U.S. bases in Jordan suggests that Tehran has been rebuilding its strike capabilities — capabilities that Mr. Trump had claimed were destroyed. As neither Washington nor Iran seems ready to step back from the precipice, the war is set to enter a more dangerous phase with global economic implications.

editorials.title: Ray of hope: On courts and reflexive arrests
editorials.passage:
The district administration in Noida, Uttar Pradesh, went to great lengths to detain 25-year-old Delhi University law student and activist Akriti Chaudhary on April 11, 2026, in connection with protests by workers in the city . But on September 2, the Allahabad High Court quashed her National Security Act (NSA) detention , terming it an “abuse of the draconian preventive detention law” and came down heavily on the administration. The High Court’s intervention is a silver lining in the dark cloud of extreme executive arbitrariness that is smothering the democratic soul of India. It termed the Noida administration’s conduct “despotic”, its allegations against the activist a “concocted story”, and noted that the District Magistrate had passed the NSA detention order “without application of mind”. Without mincing words, the High Court warned that an unhinged bureaucracy could reduce the State of Uttar Pradesh to an “Orwellian dystopia”. The Division Bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev ordered compensation of ₹5 lakh for Ms. Chaudhary, which is to be deducted from the salaries of the officers concerned. The facts of the case were brazenly in contradiction with the claims of the police and the district administration, but it also took a rigorous and conscientious Bench to provide this relief. It noted in its order that Ms. Chaudhary was already in the custody of the police when the violence that she is accused of took place.

The relief from the High Court has not set the activist free, as she is named by the U.P. Police in 11 other cases. It will be a long journey of legal battles to get her the freedom that every citizen in a democratic country deserves. That the police would go to such an extent to make life difficult for someone who stood up for the underprivileged must shock the conscience of the nation. Between April 10 and 18, 2026, industrial and contractual workers in Noida had staged protests demanding a wage hike and wage parity with neighbouring Haryana. On April 13, the protests allegedly turned violent. The Noida Police claimed to have “strong electronic and videographic evidence” of incitement against Ms. Chaudhary, and it turned out to be merely that, a claim which could not be established. Ms. Chaudhary could receive legal support and media attention that hundreds of others in comparable situations cannot easily access, while the workers remain trapped in miserable conditions because of oppressive business models and state policies that favour capital owners, with the promises made to them still unfulfilled. Yet, the Allahabad High Court’s intervention in Ms. Chaudhary’s case is a ray of hope that democratic protests will be heeded rather than suppressed by the strong-arm tactics of the executive.

editorials.title: A little silence, please: Authorities must act as noise taking lives
editorials.passage: What could be more shockingly symptomatic of India’s noise pollution epidemic than a violent mob silencing a musician who protested loudness? The death of Chongtham Vikram Singh, a Manipuri musician in Delhi, at the hands of a mob that included an adolescent boy is the latest extreme manifestation of a growing disregard for the health and peace of others among Indians who equate celebration with loud noise. The disturbing irony in Singh’s case was compounded by the silence of his neighbours as he was chased and beaten near his apartment.The 47-year-old musician’s death was not an isolated incident. Loud music has become de rigueur at private functions and communal festivals, while complaints against it are increasingly provoking violent reactions. Last week, 45-year-old Satish Sharma succumbed to injuries sustained after he was pushed down a staircase following his complaint about loud music from a neighbour’s house in Noida. Pune-based civic activist Vidyanand Bapat was assaulted on camera after complaining about loud DJ music during Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations. Several instances of mob violence were also reported during recent Kanwariya yatras against those protesting ear-splitting music played on stacked sound systems..Yet India has long recognised noise pollution as a public health hazard. Ambient noise was officially recognised as a pollutant in 2006 and, in 2011, the Central Pollution Control Board announced a National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network. However, a study published in Nature earlier this year found that Indian cities are growing harmfully louder, including around hospitals, schools and residential areas. The World Health Organization has warned that prolonged exposure to excessive noise can contribute to cardiovascular disease, sleep disruption, cognitive fatigue, and poorer work and school performance. The warnings, evidently, have fallen on deaf ears.The official apathy is appalling. This March, the government informed the Lok Sabha that it had not conducted any study to measure the health impact of car honking and loudspeaker noise, despite its own department recommending such research. Loud noise particularly affects expectant mothers, young children and the elderly. The authorities must stop merely paying lip service to a growing public health hazard and strictly enforce rules governing both the decibel levels and permitted hours of noise. Celebrations cannot become a licence to rob others of their health, sleep and peace. editorials.title: Extreme cases revitalise call of men's commission
editorials.passage: It would seem that women have it all—the fears, tears, laws, commissions, rights organisations and even a globally commemorated Women’s Day. However, some argue that as the pink tide turns more forceful, men are increasingly feeling the blues. This supposed imbalance may have prompted Karnataka State Commission for Women chairperson Nagalakshmi Chowdhary to propose a men’s commission to address the sterner sex’s complaints regarding persecution, and lopsided divorce and custody laws. Harassed men will vouch they have little institutional support by way of forums or legal aid. As the gender divide closes ever-so-slowly with greater education, financial independence and empowerment for women—aided by the internet for some—it seems that the alpha male is on the retreat. Fewer young Indians are supporting restrictive partriarchal norms, even though such deep-rooted biases show up every now and then.Meanwhile, several Indian men claim they are victims of an unfair legal system with laws like the Penal Code’s Section 498A (dowry harassment; Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) and often spend years fighting false cases. They are denied child custody and endure emotional abuse even while fulfilling financial obligations. Even the Supreme Court noted the increasing misuse of anti-dowry laws and restrained the police from automatically arresting husbands and their kin..Though the idea of a men’s commission is not new, it has found fresh currency after the alleged murders of Raja Raghuvanshi in Meghalaya and Ketan Agarwal near Lonavala. Last December, Rajya Sabha member Ashok Kumar Mittal moved a private member’s Bill for a men’s commission to protect the “rights and welfare of men”, “review existing laws and policies” and look at “issues impacting men’s physical, mental and social well-being”. In Kerala, former Congress MLA Eldhose Kunnappilly had also proposed a similar commission. A petition in the Supreme Court in 2023 seeking guidelines to address men’s harassment highlighted government data that a large number of those who had taken their own lives in 2021 were married men. It reminds us of Atul Subhash, a 34-year-old Bengaluru techie who died by suicide in 2024 after years of harassment by his wife and her family. There are many Atuls waiting for justice. That’s why gender equality campaigners claim that a men’s commission for India is an idea whose time has come..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Cruel planet of apes
editorials.passage: Indian internet has been smitten by videos of furry, orange babies with sleepy eyes rolling on a forest floor. The discovery of five orangutan babies in the Udayapur-Talsari forest on the Odisha-West Bengal border has elicited plenty of oohs and aahs all around. They are now being cared for by Odisha forest officials at Nandankanan zoo. Beyond that, there are some serious whys and hows to answer on the endangered primates’ presence thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat in southeast Asian rainforests. Experts’ apprehension that this was a smuggling operation gone awry begs questions of the network and route. Odisha’s lessons from anti-poaching initiatives must be put to work more widely—it pays to train and incentivise locals along known smuggling routes to alert officials in time..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Time to stop this charade
editorials.passage:
Seven people have now died in Satya Niketan. Six died in Saket barely three months earlier. How many more bodies does Delhi need before the government stops announcing inquiries and starts preventing deaths? As is the ritual that follows any tragedy big enough to reach TV studios and evening debates, some officials have been suspended. This time Rakesh Kumar, the Deputy Commissioner South Zone, Ranveer Singh, Superintendent Engineer South Zone, Lalit Kumar Goel Executive Engineer (Building) South Zone, Sunil Chauhan-Assistant Engineer (Building) South zone and Ashish Kumar -Junior Engineer (Building) South Zone have been suspended. 

The building owner went on the run and was arrested from Rajasthan. Had such action been taken after the previous collapses, the lives of seven people would have been saved. The blame game has already begun: labourers who worked on the reconstruction are accused of “destroying” the main pillar. Delhi continues to bury people under buildings that should have been inspected, sealed or demolished. The BBC reported that Delhi witnessed more than 1,000 building collapses in three years. 

That is not an accident rate. It is a governance record. It is the statistical signature of a city where illegal construction flourishes, inspections are delayed, warnings disappear into files and officials discover danger only after concrete has crushed human beings. A building collapses, people die and politicians arrive on the spot shedding crocodile tears. Officials announce an inquiry; the police register an FIR and the civic body issues notices. 

Once the TV cameras leave, the rubble is cleared and the system returns to its preferred state: paralysis without accountability. On September 6, a five-storey building b eing used as a b oys’ paying-guest accommodation in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University’s South Campus collapsed during repair work, killing seven. The building, reportedly about five decades old, stood in one of Delhi’s most crowded student-rental neighbourhoods. This was not an unforeseeable natural disaster. The precise chain of structural failure must be established by investigators. 

But the larger failure is already clear: Delhi has a chronic problem of unauthorised construction, unsafe buildings, illegal additions and a grotesque gap between what the authorities know and what they do. The most damning comparison is not with some distant tragedy. It is with Saket, on May 30. Six people died there too when a multi-storey building in Saidulajab collapsed. The victims included five young medical and engineering graduates. Delhi Police had written to the MCD twice in March about illegal construction at the site. The warnings existed. The authorities knew. The building remained standing until it did what dangerous buildings eventually do: it fell. 
The Supreme Court was later given an even more damning account. A status report by court-appointed amicus curiae Senior Advocate Ajit Kumar Sinha said the MCD had known about unauthorised construction at the site since 2015 but had taken no concrete action. The magisterial inquiry followed. Its findings were devastating. The MCD was held “primarily responsible” for the Saket tragedy. It was reportedly found that the collapse was preventable, identified unauthorised structural additions and said the civic body failed to act on a complaint received on March 9. 

The inquiry found no record of inspection, verification, demolition or preventive action for more than two months. It also raised allegations that official records had been fabricated to conceal lapses. So, what did the government learn from Saket? Just that another inquiry was needed. After the Saket deaths, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta ordered a citywide audit of unauthorised constructions. The MCD announced action, the mayor vowed that senior officials would face consequences and the Lieutenant Governor directed the civic body to enforce building bye-laws through a time-bound strategy. Barely three months later, seven more are dead under another building. 

This is the reason why the language of condolence now sounds less like governance and more like mockery. The Satya Niketan collapse exposes the economics of student housing. These were not luxury tenants who could demand structural certificates before signing a lease. Students come to Delhi for universities, coaching centres and jobs. They rent whatever they can afford. Landlords subdivide buildings. Floors are added. Basements are altered. Rooms are packed with people far beyond the capacity for which the structure was designed. When housing is scarce and expensive, overcrowding stops looking like an outrage to the rental market. It becomes a business model. The state’s responsibility begins here. A landlord may be criminally liable for an illegal alteration. 

That must be established by investigation and prosecution. But the government remains politically accountable for allowing an ecosystem of illegal construction and unsafe rental housing to flourish. The MCD’s action next door makes the failure impossible to disguise. After the Satya Niketan collapse, the civic body found the adjoining House No. 13 in a “ruinous, dangerous condition” and ordered its occupants to vacate and the structure to be demolished within three days. If a building can be declared dangerous within three days after its neighbour collapses, why did it require a death next door to become visible? This is not an argument against demolition but an indictment of waiting. The MCD has reportedly ordered the sealing of illegally constructed buildings of more than four floors across Delhi. 

That sounds decisive, but Delhi has heard decisive announcements before. The problem is not the absence of orders. It is the absence of consequences when orders are ignored. Delhi Police had flagged the Saket construction before the collapse but MCD did not act. The inquiry found that the civic body failed in its responsibility. This is not merely a story about a rogue builder. It is a story about the deadly distance between a warning being received and an official being compelled to act. That distance is where people die. The same questions must now be asked about Satya Niketan. Who knew about the state of the building? Who inspected its illegal construction? 

Was the basement work authorised? Who approved its use as a PG accommodation? How many occupants was it legally permitted to house? Were complaints made? Were structural alterations reported? What action was taken and if none was taken, why not? These questions cannot be buried beneath an FIR against the owner. The elected representative must also answer political questions. Satya Niketan falls in the R.K. Puram Assembly constituency, represented by BJP MLA Anil Kumar Sharma. The MLA is not a building inspector and cannot personally certify every structure in his constituency. But he is supposed to be the political eyes and ears of the people who elected him. If illegal PGs, unsafe buildings and unauthorised alterations are widespread in the constituency, what did he know? What did he raise? What did he demand from the MCD? These are questions of p ublic accountability, not allegations of personal criminal liability. A government that campaigns on the platform of change cannot ask citizens to wait while its departments learn how to govern. Rekha Gupta has ordered a magisterial inquiry into Satya Niketan and directed an FIR against the building owner. Those steps are necessary. They are not enough. The danger is obvious: the inquiry becomes another place where responsibility goes to die. The SDM belongs to the Delhi government’s administrative structure. The MCD is responsible for civic enforcement. The police have their own jurisdiction. Files move between offices. Notices are issued. Replies are sought. Committees meet. Courts intervene. Years pass. This is how accountability disappears: not because nobody is responsible, but because responsibility is divided among enough institutions for everyone to claim that somebody else was responsible. The public is left with the rubble. The government should do something different this time. Put the investigation under independent judicial oversight. The Supreme Court is already examining illegal construction and civic failure in Delhi. Its court-appointed amicus has sought structural audits and time-bound demolition or sealing of illegal structures. The government should seek court-monitored compliance with a citywide safety audit. 

The audit must publish the list of dangerous buildings, set deadlines for action, name the officials responsible and require periodic public reports. The principle is brutally simple: Identify. Act. Report. Not identify, constitute a committee, issue a notice, seek a reply, lose the file, discover another jurisdiction and wait for the building to collapse. Delhi does not need another inquiry into why buildings collapse. It needs an inquiry into why warnings do not produce action. The only solution: Perform or Go. Six people died in Saket in June. Seven more died in Satya Niketan. 

The next inquiry will not bring them back. The only meaningful question left is whether this government can prevent the next lot of victims perishing in the rubble of apathy and corruption. 

The writer is Editor-in-chief, Asia Features News Service

editorials.title: Whither Punjab?
editorials.passage:
Punjab, the land of revolutions, is approaching another election with a familiar problem ~ it has plenty of Chief Minister aspirants, plenty of political activity, and remarkably little evidence of a new political idea. With State Assembly Election approaching, all major parties appear increasingly preoccupied with themselves. Factionalism, dissidence, rival camps and leadership ambitions dominate political discourse across the spectrum. 

That would be merely tiresome were Punjab not confronting a formidable collection of problems. Its agricultural model is straining under the weight of groundwater depletion, abject soil degradation, and economic stagnation. Its industrial towns like Ludhiana or Rajpura have lost the dynamism that once made them synonymous with enterprise. Its young people increasingly look abroad for opportunity. Its public finances leave little room for grand experiments. And Punjab has yet to produce a convincing account of what its economy should look like after the era of wheat, rice, and remittances. The 2026–27 budget projects a revenue deficit of Rs 21,955 crore and a fiscal deficit of Rs 39,971 crore, or 4.1 per cent of GSDP. Agriculture is expected to contract by 2.5 per cent. 

These figures ought to be the raw material for a political renaissance. Instead, they have become the backdrop to an increasingly inward-looking politics. Punjab’s political parties seem to have discovered that the easiest election to contest is the one against their own colleagues. Congress has rival camps and competing ambitions. The BJP is trying to consolidate itself after its separation from the Shiromani Akali Dal. The Akalis are fighting to recover lost political space. The Aam Aadmi Party, once the insurgent outsider, is now defending its record while managing its own pressures (including defections). The spectacle increasingly resembles an American primary, except there is no primary. 

Aspiring leaders campaign against their colleagues, cultivate factions, and position themselves for the nomination while the electorate waits for someone to explain what happens after the election. There is an even more remarkable feature i.e., unbelievable ideological elasticity. Parties that spend months denouncing one another can discover, with astonishing speed, reasons to share a platform when arithmetic demands it. The renewed speculation about a possible SAD-BJP alliance is merely the latest reminder of how fluid Punjab’s political calculations have become. The permutations are almost mathematical ~ Akalis with BJP, Congress with AAP, AAP with Akalis, combinations before polling and combinations after it. The only fixed principle seems to be that nothing is fixed. There is, in other words, no obvious “party with a difference”. The parties increasingly resemble one another in the one respect that matters most to their leaders ~ the pursuit of power. Ideology is negotiable. 

Loyalties are portable. Poaching has become routine. Political opponents can become coalition partners with remarkable speed. The question is less What should Punjab become? than Who gets to run it? Punjab once had a remarkably clear sense of purpose. The Green Revolution transformed its agriculture and helped transform India. Its farmers became central to national food security. Ludhiana and other industrial centres developed formidable clusters of engineering, bicycles, textiles, machine tools and manufacturing. Its young men filled the armed forces and other uniformed services. Its people acquired a reputation for enterprise and confidence. That confidence has weakened. 

The most disturbing sign may not be any single statistic but the changing aspirations of the young. For an earlier generation, the dream was to become a soldier, officer, doctor, engineer, sportsperson, entrepreneur or professional and to build a life in Punjab. Increasingly, the dream seems simpler - Get qualified, get out. Migration is not inherently a failure. Punjab's diaspora is one of its greatest assets. But when a state exports a disproportionate share of its young, educated and ambitious citizens because they see better prospects elsewhere, the problem becomes developmental. A state can survive the departure of some of its people. It cannot indefinitely survive the departure of its aspirations. All this should provide fertile ground for political parties to abandon tired scripts and offer something genuinely progressive. 

There is plenty to campaign about e.g., how to diversify agriculture without impoverishing farmers; restore groundwater; revive Ludhiana and other industrial centres; attract new manufacturing and services; improve universities and skills; increase women’s participation in the economy, and turn the diaspora into a source of investment and knowledge rather than merely an exit route. And there is the largest question of all ~ how to do this while carrying a heavy fiscal burden? These problems cannot be solved by another electricity subsidy, cash transfer or slogan. Yet freebies are politically irresistible precisely because structural reform is not. A transfer can be announced at a rally. Building a new industrial ecosystem takes years. A subsidy fits neatly into a manifesto. Reforming agriculture requires political courage. Punjab therefore risks a vicious circle: Weak growth → demand for transfers → less fiscal space → less productive investment → weaker growth. At some point, the state risks becoming very good at distributing the proceeds of an economy it has stopped rebuilding. 

This is where comparison with an earlier Punjab becomes painful. Whatever their shortcomings, leaders such as Pratap Singh Kairon and Parkash Singh Badal belonged to a political tradition in which personal relationships could survive political disagreement and public purpose could sometimes rise above partisan calculation. They understood that politics was a contest between competing visions, not necessarily permanent personal warfare. That tradition now seems distant. Today’s political class appears increasingly skilled at faction management, defections, tactical alliances and political positioning. It is much harder to identify an equivalent sense of long-term mission. 

Yet Punjab needs precisely that. It needs leaders prepared to tell farmers uncomfortable truths about water and cropping patterns; industrialists what must change to compete; young people why staying can be worthwhile; voters why every promise has a cost; and politicians themselves that public money cannot indefinitely substitute for public policy. That requires political courage and patience ~ qualities that sit awkwardly with the obsession with the next election. Punjab is, after all, the ancient land of revolutionaries. Its history is crowded with people prepared to challenge established authority, accept sacrifice and imagine something larger than themselves. Its political culture was once animated by the conviction that public life could transform society. 

The irony today is almost cruel - the land of revolutionaries is being consumed by its own “revolutionary” leadership! The parties still speak the language of change. The slogans remain grand. But beneath the noise is a striking absence of ambition for anything beyond political survival. Perhaps the real revolution Punjab needs is therefore not another party, another leader or another rearrangement of alliances. It is a clean break with a political culture in which power has become an end in itself; ideology can be exchanged for arithmetic; personal ambition overwhelms public purpose, and parties that have spent months attacking one another can discover a common cause when the numbers require it. 

The silver lining is difficult to see. But perhaps it lies outside the political class. Punjab’s electorate has repeatedly shown that it can surprise its politicians. Great political changes rarely come from comfortable establishments. They come when ordinary people decide that the existing arrangement no longer represents their aspirations. The question now is whether that instinct can return. Punjab does not need politicians clever enough merely to win the next election. It needs leaders ambitious enough to make Punjab itself the object of their ambition. That would be a revolution worth having. 

(The writer is Lt Gen PVSM, AVSM (Retd), and former Lt Governor of Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Puducherry)

editorials.title: Flexible approach to sugarcane needed
editorials.passage:
The sugar in India’s kitchen and the fuel in its cars increasingly have something in common: sugarcane. India’s ethanol programme is altering the economics of a crop that already has to satisfy the country’s enormous appetite for sugar. With domestic production now expected to fall well below previous estimates, the government has opened duty-free imports to ease pressure on the market. Ethanol is not the sole reason for the current shortage, but it has added another demand for sugarcane. 

The crop now has to meet demand for sugar, ethanol and exports. When production falls short, producers need room to adapt to changing market conditions. The immediate problem is clear. India’s sugar production is now expected to be around 30.6 million tonnes, significantly below the government’s earlier estimate of 34.4 million tonnes. Exports were approved before the scale of the shortfall became clear, with around 800,000 tonnes shipped before restrictions were imposed. The result is a tighter domestic market and higher prices at a time when demand is expected to rise ahead of the festive season. 

The decision to allow an additional one million tonnes of raw sugar into the country duty-free should provide consumers and businesses with another source of supply. The Food Secretary has subsequently said ex-mill sugar prices fell 18 per cent to Rs 55 per kilogram, although that reduction has not yet fully reached retail consumers. The move is a useful reminder that when domestic supply falls short, access to international markets can provide some relief. But India’s sugar market is shaped by more than supply and demand. 

Sugarcane supports the livelihoods of millions of farmers, provides sugar for domestic consumption, contributes to exports and now serves as feedstock for ethanol. Under the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme, oil marketing companies procure ethanol for blending with petrol at government-set prices, creating another market for sugarcane beyond sugar production. The government has also supported investment in ethanol capacity. The programme aims to reduce crude oil imports, strengthen energy security and create another source of demand for the sugar industry. 

These are valid objectives. The challenge is managing these demands when they all depend on the same crop. Nearly three million tonnes of sugar were diverted towards ethanol production this year, prompting debate over whether fuel demand is contributing to tighter sugar supplies. The government, however, argues that the share of sugarcane diverted to ethanol has fallen from around 12 per cent in 2022-23 to roughly 9 per cent in 2025-26. 

That disagreement matters. The question is not whether India should produce ethanol, but whether producers have enough flexibility to respond when the balance between sugar, fuel and export demand changes. Brazil offers a useful example. Its large sugar-ethanol industry gives mills the ability to respond to market conditions. When sugar prices are more attractive, more cane can be directed towards sugar. When ethanol demand is stronger, mills can shift more towards fuel. India does not need to choose between the two. 

But producers need room to respond when circumstances change. When sugar supplies tighten, restricting exports may help keep more sugar in the domestic market in the short term. But it cannot make up for a weaker crop. If production is lower than expected, stopping exports does not create more sugar. It can instead make it harder for farmers, mills and traders to plan, while consumers are left to absorb the higher prices that come with tighter supply. 

The same principle applies to imports. India should not have to wait for prices to surge before allowing global markets to act as a safety valve. If domestic production falls short, access to international supply can prevent a temporary shortage from becoming a prolonged price shock. Open trade does not replace domestic production; it gives the market another way to respond when forecasts prove wrong. Food security matters. So do farmer incomes and energy security. 

But pursuing these goals does not require policymakers to decide exactly where every tonne of sugarcane should go. India can expand ethanol while maintaining a reliable sugar supply. The key is giving farmers and mills enough flexibility to respond to changing conditions, while ensuring consumers are not left paying the price when policy or production forecasts get it wrong. The writer is Indian Policy Associate, Consumer Choice Center.

editorials.title: The Firewall
editorials.passage:
Germany’s political establishment has spent years treating Alternative für Deutschland as a problem that could be contained by isolation. Saxony-Anhalt suggests that strategy is approaching its limits. The AfD’s emphatic victory in the eastern German state has not given it an outright parliamentary majority. Yet that may make the result more politically consequential, not less. The party has won enough support to claim a mandate while leaving its opponents with the awkward responsibility of preventing the largest party from governing. Germany’s celebrated Brandmauer ~ the political firewall against cooperation with the far right ~ is now facing its most serious practical test. The dilemma cannot be dismissed simply by invoking democratic arithmetic. 

Elections determine representation; they do not oblige parties to form governments with ideological opponents. Mainstream German parties have legitimate reasons for refusing cooperation with an organisation whose regional branches have been classified by domestic intelligence authorities as right-wing extremist. But neither can the political meaning of such a large vote be wished away. A firewall is an instrument of containment, not a substitute for politics. It can keep a party outside government; it cannot explain why voters increasingly put it first. 

That is the uncomfortable message for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Germany’s mainstream centre-right. The CDU has tried to compete with the AfD by toughening its language on immigration while maintaining an absolute prohibition on cooperation. Saxony-Anhalt indicates that this balancing act may be failing. Voters seeking a harder alternative appear increasingly inclined to choose the original rather than a moderated imitation. The danger for Germany’s established parties lies in confusing exclusion with defeat. If the AfD remains permanently shut out despite repeatedly winning or dominating elections, it can continue presenting itself as the victim of an insulated political establishment. 

Every blocked path to power can become further evidence for its central argument: that the system listens to voters only when they vote for approved parties. Conversely, bringing the AfD into government would expose it to a challenge it has largely avoided. Protest politics thrives on identifying failure; governing requires accepting responsibility for difficult trade-offs. Control of a state administration, policing and education would test whether the party’s promises can survive contact with institutional and constitutional constraints. This is why Saxony-Anhalt matters beyond one relatively small eastern state. Across Europe, nationalist parties are moving from the margins towards the centre of electoral politics. 

The question confronting established democracies is no longer merely how to condemn them, but how to respond when millions of voters demonstrably prefer them. Germany’s history gives its political firewall a particular moral and historical weight. But history alone cannot provide an electoral strategy. The defence of democratic institutions requires more than a refusal to cooperate with those regarded as hostile to them. It also requires understanding why confidence in established parties has eroded so profoundly. Saxony-Anhalt has exposed the weakness of a strategy built principally around keeping AfD out. The firewall may still be standing. Whether the political foundations beneath it remain secure is another matter.

editorials.title: Hidden vulnerability
editorials.passage:
India's ambitions of becoming a global digital power rest on an infrastructure paradox. The country has embraced cheap data, built one of the world’s largest online populations and is rapidly expanding its data-centre capacity. It now speaks confidently of artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure and technological sovereignty. Yet a significant part of the physical network connecting this digital economy to the world remains concentrated, ageing and dependent on capabilities India does not control. 

This is not a hypothetical weakness. International data does not travel through satellites floating harmlessly above geopolitical tensions. Almost all of it moves through fibre-optic cables laid across the ocean floor. Damage to these cables is commonplace, caused by anchors, fishing activity, natural events and equipment failures. Deliberate sabotage has become an additional concern as geopolitical competition increasingly extends to critical infrastructure. India’s particular problem is concentration. A large share of its westward international connectivity comes ashore within a small stretch of Mumbai’s coastline. Networks can reroute traffic when individual cables fail, but redundancy should not be confused with resilience. Rerouting can degrade performance, increase costs and place pressure on alternative routes. For an economy increasingly dependent on real-time financial transactions, cloud computing and AI applications, even partial disruption can have consequences far beyond an inconvenience to internet users. 

The more revealing vulnerability lies in India’s inability to repair its own subsea cables. A fault in Indian waters can require foreign repair vessels to be deployed from hubs such as Dubai or Singapore, followed by regulatory permissions to operate. This exposes a familiar weakness in India’s approach to infrastructure: enormous attention to construction and expansion, but insufficient planning for maintenance, resilience and emergency response. The mismatch could become more serious as India builds data centres at remarkable speed. Computing capacity can be installed relatively quickly; international connectivity cannot. 

Planning and laying submarine cables takes years, while landing stations involve a maze of approvals across multiple ministries and agencies. If the physical arteries of the digital economy expand more slowly than the demand placed upon them, India could create impressive computing capacity without ensuring equally reliable connections to global networks. The answer is not technological nationalism. India need not own every cable connecting it to the world. But it must reduce excessive geographic concentration, create more landing points, simplify approvals and develop domestic repair capability. Island territories and both coastlines offer opportunities for greater route diversity. 

Digital sovereignty is often discussed in terms of data localisation, domestic platforms and indigenous AI. But sovereignty also has a more prosaic physical meaning. A country aspiring to be a digital power must be able to protect, maintain and rapidly repair the infrastructure on which its digital future depends. India’s internet revolution may be visible on billions of screens. Its greatest vulnerability, for now, remains hidden beneath the sea.

editorials.title: Be answerable
editorials.passage:
There is something conspicuously absent from public life in India: accountability. Whether an institution is public or private, its functionaries are primarily accountable upwards — to their organisational hierarchy, political masters, owners or regulators. The people who are supposed to be the ultimate beneficiaries — forget constitutional sovereigns — of public institutions are usually at the receiving end. They have little voice, still less recourse, when those institutions fail them.

Education provides perhaps the starkest illustration.

For decades, commission after commission has recognised that India cannot become an educated and equitable society without substantially increasing public expenditure on education. The Kothari Commission recommended that expenditure should reach 6% of GDP. The target was reiterated by successive education policies and, most recently, by the National Education Policy, 2020. Yet it has never been achieved. Combined Centre-and-state expenditure on education has hovered around 2.8%-2.9% of GDP since 2015, according to the parliamentary research service; the Economic Survey put it at only 2.7% in 2023-24.

So much for education being the foundation of a knowledge economy, the pathway to Viksit Bharat!

The consequences are visible everywhere. India’s public-school system, which serves the overwhelming majority of children from poorer households, has been allowed to deteriorate while private education has expanded into a huge, parallel market. Government policy increasingly speaks the language of rationalisation: schools with small enrolments are merged or closed in the name of efficiency. The education ministry itself has parliamentary material dealing with the closure and rationalisation of government schools. But what looks efficient on an administrative spreadsheet can be devastating for a child who must now travel several kilometres to attend school — or simply drop out.

The dropout figures remain disturbing. According to UDISE+ 2024–25, the national dropout rate was 11.5% at the secondary level, compared to 3.5% at the upper-primary level. And dropout is only one measure of failure. A child can remain enrolled for years and emerge without acquiring the most elementary competencies.

The latest ASER findings make that uncomfortable reality impossible to hide. In rural India, only 23.4% of Class III children could read a Class II-level text in 2024. Among Class V children in government schools, only 44.8% could do so. There has been some recovery after the pandemic, but these figures still describe an education system in which a substantial proportion of children spend years in school without acquiring foundational skills.

What happens to these children when they reach higher education? They enter a system increasingly dominated by degrees, examinations and credentials rather than learning. The result is the grotesque spectacle of millions competing for a handful of jobs while employers complain that graduates lack the skills they require. Mercer | Mettl’s 2025 Graduate Skill Index found only 42.6% of Indian graduates who apply for jobs to be overall employable. The problem, then, is not simply unemployment. It is an education system that often fails both the student and the economy.

And yet, who is accountable? When a school closes, is the education minister made accountable to the parents whose children must travel farther? When teachers are absent or posts remain vacant, who answers to the children losing their formative years? When universities deteriorate, examinations are mismanaged or recruitment is delayed, who bears responsibility? And when an examination paper leaks, why should students have to pay the price?

The recent youth movement has provided a remarkable answer: if the system will not hold itself accountable, the young will try to hold it accountable.

What began with outrage over examination irregularities and the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak grew into a nationwide youth mobilisation. Protesters remained at Jantar Mantar for weeks, demanded the resignation of the then education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, supported an indefinite hunger strike, marched towards Parliament and faced baton charges, tear gas shells, and also pellet guns from the police.

The demand was strikingly modest: someone must take responsibility.

But even that elementary principle had to be extracted from the system through sustained public pressure. On July 25, after weeks of protest, Pradhan resigned. The resignation was a significant victory precisely because ministerial accountability has become so rare.

Yet we should not mistake the resignation for the solution. A minister leaving office does not repair a broken examination system. It does not rebuild a government school. It does not train a teacher, restore a university or teach a child to read. Nor does it answer the larger question: why must citizens repeatedly take to the streets before those entrusted with public institutions accept responsibility for their failure?

This is the real issue of public accountability in education.

Education is not a commodity that can simply be purchased by those who can afford it. It is a public good and a constitutional instrument of social transformation. For the poor, for Dalits, Adivasis, women and historically excluded communities, public education is often the only route to a life different from that of their parents. To allow its quality to collapse is, therefore, not merely an administrative failure. It reproduces inequality.

Nor can the answer be to abandon public education and leave families to the private market. A government that closes schools because they are ‘uneconomical’ while millions of children remain dependent upon them has inverted the meaning of public service. The efficiency of education cannot be measured merely by the number of schools closed, teachers rationalised or rupees saved. The measure is what children learn, whether they remain in school, whether they acquire capabilities, and whether education expands their freedom.

India has no shortage of policies, commissions, committees, slogans or grand declarations about becoming a knowledge superpower. What it lacks is the most elementary ingredient of a functioning democracy: someone answerable when the promise is not delivered.

The young people who came onto the streets have raised a question much larger than a paper leak. They have challenged a political culture in which institutions answer to their superiors but not to the people they exist to serve. That may ultimately be the most important lesson of the movement.

Education does not merely need more money. It needs accountability — and accountability begins when those who exercise power can no longer evade responsibility to those in whose name they exercise it.

Anand Teltumbde is a scholar and civil rights activist

editorials.title: Where the mind is with fear
editorials.passage:
Conceptually, institutional autonomy and academic freedom are distinct. But both are in peril — globally, not just in India. In Hungary, the Central European University was forced to relocate to Vienna after the then Hungarian government passed legislation effectively banning it from operating in Budapest. The underlying reason was adversarial politics. The Donald Trump administration felt Harvard was excessively “woke”, Left-leaning and hostile to conservative viewpoints and demanded changes to its governance, admissions, hiring and academic programmes. A book titled Academic Freedom in the Era of Trump has analysed the history of academic freedom in the United States of America and its recent demise. The American Association of University Professors has argued in its recent report that the Trump administration has weaponised federal civil rights laws with the goal of discrediting colleges and compromising their academic freedom and institutional autonomy.

India is also witnessing erosion of institutional autonomy and academic freedom, manifested primarily in increasing political interference in university governance, pressure to introduce specific courses, interference in contents of syllabi and intimidation of outspoken academics. The Government of India believes that in Jawaharlal Nehru University, dissent expressed by a section of students and faculty has crossed into anti-nationalism. An ongoing tussle, widely reported in the press, concerns a Bill introduced in Parliament that seeks to repeal the Indian Statistical Institute Act of 1959 and bring several aspects of the governance of this Institution of National Importance under greater Central control. The proposed centralisation and the streamlining measures will result in the erosion of institutional autonomy and, consequently, academic freedom.

An update of the Academic Freedom Index was published in March this year. The report stated that academic freedom has been increasingly under attack, both in scale and intensity. The number of countries (50) that witnessed a decline of academic freedom vastly outnumbered those that witnessed an improvement (9). “Fast and steep deterioration” of institutional autonomy was noted in the US. Significant effects of democratic backsliding of institutions in India in the last decade due to the increasing power of “anti-pluralist” political forces in limiting academic freedom have also been noted. India now occupies 156th place out of 179 countries, as per AFI. The AFI rated many countries, including India, as “completely restricted” with respect to academic freedom.

It is ironic that India should occupy such a low place in spite of an early recognition of and emphasis on institutional autonomy and academic freedom. In the famous speech that Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee delivered to the Senate of the University of Calcutta in 1922, he said “I call upon you, as members of the Senate to stand up for the rights of your University. Forget the Government of India. Do your duty as Senators of the University, as true sons of your Alma Mater. Freedom first, freedom second and freedom always – nothing else will satisfy me.” The Kothari Commission report of 1966 stated “… that only an autonomous institution, free from regimentation of ideas and pressure of party or power politics, can pursue truth fearlessly and build up, in its teachers and students, habits of independent thinking and a spirit of enquiry unfettered by the limitations and prejudices of the near and the immediate which is so essential for the development of a free society.”

Academic freedom considers the rights to teach and to learn as vital and inseparable. Interfering with these imperils the right of the teacher to teach as well as the right of the student to learn. The UN Human Rights Council has considered scholarship, teaching, and institutional autonomy as fundamental human rights. Yet, the 2025 annual report by the Scholars at Risk Network has noted that “In India, a number of universities put in place new policies that limited student expression by banning students from holding discussions, demonstrations, or sloganeering without prior authorization.” Ironically, India is a signatory, along with 72 other nations, of a 2023 joint statement on academic freedom presented during the 52nd session of the United Human Rights Council. The statement noted: “Without academic freedom, there is no safeguard against the manipulation of information or against the distortion of history. Regrettably, attacks on academic freedom are on the rise. These include: repression, intimidation and harassment of researchers and teachers in connection with their research and public statements; dissolution of research institutions and the establishment of restrictive legal or financial frameworks.”The Bharatiya Janata Party is India’s dominant political force now. It should have greater confidence in the resilience of the institutions it governs. It should encourage and allow — not enforce — institutions to overhaul and develop. Fear of disagreement, criticism, or independent thinking within academic institutions cannot be in the DNA of a confident political party.

Academic institutions should be free to pursue research, debate contentious questions and appoint scholars on academic merit. Such an environment is essential for producing the knowledge, innovation and talent that India needs. If the BJP believes that its vision for the country has broad intellectual and social merit, it should welcome scrutiny rather than seek conformity. Protecting institutional autonomy and academic freedom should, therefore, not be seen as a concession to political opponents. Instead, it would indicate an affirmation of confidence in India’s democratic institutions, its scholars and, ultimately, in the strength of the BJP’s own ideas.

Partha P. Majumder is Emeritus Professor, Indian Statistical Institute

editorials.title: Fault lines resurface
editorials.passage:
One of the many thorny issues raised by the ethnic crisis in Manipur is this: who is a tribal and who qualifies as a scheduled tribe. The demand by a section of the largely Hindu Meitei community for this status was the trigger for the outbreak of the complicated, multi-dimensional conflict in the state. A rally on May 3, 2023, by Nagas and Kukis in the hill districts against a Manipur High Court order directing the state government not to hinder official scrutiny of this Meitei demand had seemed like just another manifestation of the state’s endemic hill-valley divide. But this presumption proved false. The rally turned violent in the Kuki-Zo-dominated Churachandpur district and began spreading. What no keen observer should have missed, but most did, was that at this point the Nagas stepped back. Although the demand by Meiteis for ST status was the trigger, there were other cinders waiting to catch flames.

By February this year, this oversight became glaring. Even as the feud between Meiteis and Kukis showed signs of abating, a new conflict front opened up between Nagas and Kukis which has since seen some gruesome massacres. The issue on this front is more primordial too, and thus more challenging. It involves primal notions of indigenous land and its control. Nagas claim they are the original owners of the hills and Kukis settled here later with Naga permission and thus Naga customary laws are binding on all in these hills. Customary laws, however, differ from community to community, and often are at cross-purposes. If in the hills the clash is of customary laws, in the hills-valley divide, the fault line is between spheres under modern land laws and those in the realm of customary laws. Colonial administrators in Assam and the Northeast took the easy way out, drawing an Inner Line by the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873, to divide hills from plains. In Bodhisattva Kar’s words in “When Was the Postcolonial?: A History of Policing Impossible Lines”, this was not only a dividing line in territorial terms but also in time, for it divided “pre-capital” and “capital”, “‘no law’” and “‘law’”. The territories beyond this Inner Line were kept either as backward tracts, unadministered areas, excluded areas or partially-excluded areas. Administration in the hills was generally left to the devices of local communities, albeit under the governor’s gaze, while the plains were directly administered under existing laws. Although not formally as in Assam, this pattern of administration was replicated in the erstwhile princely state of Manipur.

Independent India inherited this legacy. In the nearly 80 years since then, this administrative gulf between hills and plains became institutionalised, buttressed by a liberal reservation policy. Curiously, this is a factor in the current crisis in Manipur. Similar crises can explode anywhere in the region. Meghalaya recently demonstrated how fragile this balance is, although thankfully sanity prevailed early this time. The truth is that social conditions do not remain stagnant and societies grow and transition out of past traps. When this is presumed not to be the case, there are consequences. There is now a growing number who also want to enjoy the benefits of this asymmetric policy architecture as it has come to be seen not as a lift for the weak, but as a privilege. If Meiteis are demanding ST status in Manipur, in Assam there are six previously non-tribal communities that also want to be in the ST category. It is anybody’s guess how many more would be joining this chorus in later years.

If those who now want to be in this category do so for the preferential benefits, those already in it opposing others entering it do so for the same reason. They want to prevent others from sharing their reserved pie. Otherwise, growth in the size of any fraternity should have been a matter of rejoicing for everybody within it. The trouble also is that in the name of political correctness and self-presumed generosity, there are many who still think that the idea of a tribe is permanently frozen as in a museum, not realising this can be undeclared patronising arrogance or, worse still, organic and thus invisible racism. Asymmetric policies are probably still necessary to address inequalities but the evolutionary reality of social mobility cannot be ignored in this equation.

Pradip Phanjoubam is editor, Imphal Review of Arts and Politics

editorials.title: Deep Impact: Editorial on govt intervention in inter-university transfer of Bengal teachers
editorials.passage:
The Bharatiya Janata Party government in West Bengal is concerned about higher education in the state. So the West Bengal Universities and Colleges Administration and Regulation Amendment Bill, 2026 is instituting a new system of inter-university transfers of teachers. The principle is admirable. Experienced teachers of state universities are to be transferred to fledgling universities as those in Jhargram or Cooch Behar in order to build them up to achieve excellence. The new universities would gain from the advice on infrastructure and teaching methods of senior teachers as students would gain from their learning. Transferring teachers between institutions has been the established system in government colleges, with a view to a just sharing of teachers’ learning. Teachers are recruited by the Public Service Commission and are considered to be in government service, with transfer being a condition of their job. But the same system in universities, however good in principle, begins to look different in application. Teachers are hired by each university according to its own needs. This is part of its autonomy. The new bill junks the notion of autonomy of universities and turns decisions about teacher placement over to the government. A university’s needs, the academic traditions it has created over the years with its teaching staff, the strengthening of its core competence, the welfare of its students are being considered not of any account. Evidently, the government is confident of its own expertise in academics.

An educational institution grows into excellence through years of effort. Intervention by the government through the transfer of teachers would threaten to destroy this excellence and destabilise standards, besides causing insecurity among teachers and their students. There would also be the fear of being targeted for being critical of the government. Thus the new bill would have a deep impact on the environment of universities. The space for free intellectual engagement, curiosity and exploration, diversities of opinion, continuity in research would all be affected by the uncertainty that the bill introduces. It must be asked whether transferring “experienced teachers” — who identifies them? — to new universities would guarantee their growth towards excellence. A university needs funds and infrastructure, its own goals, its areas of emphasis and the freedom to develop its resources. Each should work on its own capacities. Teachers from other universities cannot be their only means of growth.

editorials.title: Right rises: Editorial on the resurgent far-right in Europe
editorials.passage:
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has conceded that the triumph of the Alternative for Germany in the polls in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt has left his Christian Democratic Union “shaken”. Yet, the AfD’s success is not unexpected. Over a decade, the far-Right has shaped itself into a political force to reckon with, especially in some regions of what was once East Germany. What has been noticeable is the AfD’s ability to mould itself according to the shifting tide of public disaffection. The AfD’s formative years saw it mobilise against the fiscal austerity policies of the former German chancellor, Angela Merkel. Then, it quickly latched on to the ascendant, pan-European sentiment against immigration, laying bare its own controversial concept of ‘remigration’ — the ouster of all non-ethnic Germans, especially those from Islamic countries. Eastern Germany’s persistent economic woes were another fault line that Germany’s far-Right has exploited adroitly. That Centrist regimes — not only in Germany — have also struggled to ease such other challenges as price rise and inequality has augmented the AfD’s electoral clout.

Given Germany’s — and the world’s — disastrous experience with Nazism, the AfD’s recent electoral success has, quite naturally, led to jitters across Europe. It is being speculated, not without reason, that this development in Germany would have a cascading effect and strengthen extremist constituencies in poll-bound France, Spain and Italy. But it must also be pointed out that the far-Right’s ideological and electoral triumphs in Europe have been uneven. Giorgia Meloni, the poster lady of Europe’s right-wing, toned down her shrill rhetoric considerably upon assuming office; Geert Wilder’s coalition collapsed in the Netherlands because of the refusal of his allies to toe his extreme line on immigration; Reform UK has suffered electoral setbacks; Viktor Orbán has been booted out in Hungary; even the AfD fell short of the majority in Saxony-Anhalt. So resistance to the AfD and its brethren remains. But what this resistance must now acknowledge is that Europe’s resurgent far-Right is a different beast from that of the 1930s. It is much more nimble while remaining populist, and is thus able to manoeuvre past traditional ideological and profane road blocks. Consequently, it now appeals to a broader segment of the population. It is this mutated strain that is the real challenge.

editorials.title: Age shouldn’t restrict an MII chief’s tenure
editorials.passage:
India’s capital markets are deeper, more technology-driven and more closely integrated with the economy than they were a decade ago. Their infrastructure depends on speed, resilience, sophisticated surveillance and investor confidence.

Yet the regulatory framework for leading a market infrastructure institution (MII) remains rigid: its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer cannot continue beyond 65.

A more proportionate approach would make 65 the normal retirement age while permitting continuation up to 70, subject to enhanced governance assessment, performance review, succession planning and prior regulatory approval. This would preserve age as an important review point without treating it as an automatic disqualification.

The issue is not about any particular MII or its MD and CEO. It is whether the regulatory framework should recognise that, in an MII, experience can itself be an institutional asset.

MIIs provide critical financial infrastructure. They support capital formation, price discovery and liquidity, while their systems affect listed companies, investors, intermediaries and the wider financial ecosystem. The MD and CEO therefore requires a distinctive combination of capital-market knowledge, regulatory sensitivity, technological understanding, risk-management ability, crisis-handling skills and stakeholder credibility.

Much of this capability develops through exposure to market cycles, financial disruptions, regulatory changes and technological transformation. In capital markets, experience does not necessarily depreciate with age. At times, it compounds.

This is not an argument against younger leadership. It is an argument against treating chronological age as an adequate proxy for competence or fitness.

Under the present regulatory framework, the MD and CEO of an MII requires prior regulatory approval and is subject to defined tenure limits. The regulations permit a maximum of two five-year terms, subject to a maximum age of 65. These safeguards are important. But once performance, integrity, fitness and regulatory suitability are assessed, should age alone remain an absolute prohibition?

The Companies Act, 2013 provides an instructive direction. It sets a general ceiling of 70 for a managing director, whole-time director or manager, while permitting continuation beyond that age through a special resolution and appropriate disclosure. The principle is relevant: age can trigger enhanced evaluation without necessarily determining the outcome. MIIs, after all, are incorporated companies.

The regulatory framework itself offers an interesting comparison. While the MD and CEO of an MII faces a maximum age of 65, a Public Interest Director on a recognised stock exchange or clearing corporation can be nominated up to 75, subject to applicable requirements.

The roles are different and their age limits need not be identical. Yet the comparison raises a legitimate question: if a person can continue to discharge public-interest and fiduciary responsibilities on the governing board of an MII until 75, should an otherwise fit and effective MD and CEO necessarily become ineligible at 65?

The RBI provides another comparison. It permits an MD and CEO or Whole-time Director of a private-sector bank to continue up to 70, while the bank’s Board may prescribe a lower retirement age. The framework also emphasises tenure, performance review and succession planning.

The proposed Securities Market Code provides for 65 for whole-time positions and 70 for part-time positions. A five-year differential between full-time and part-time positions is thus a familiar regulatory approach. There is a case for considering whether a similar architecture could apply to MIIs — 70 for the executive head and 75 for non-executive directors.

The point is not that age limits should be uniform. It is that age need not be treated as an inflexible proxy for suitability.

Internationally, there is generally no comparable regulatory age ceiling for the professional heads of MIIs. The broader direction of travel suggests that regulation need not discard experienced leadership merely because of an arbitrary age threshold.

There is also a sound governance rationale for distinguishing executive and non-executive roles. An executive position involves continuous operational responsibility, sustained intensity and day-to-day management. A non-executive role is primarily one of oversight, deliberation and governance and can therefore be performed effectively for somewhat longer.

Regulation should not discard accumulated talent, experience and institutional wisdom merely because a person crosses a particular age. Age may be relevant to fitness and succession planning, but it is no substitute for competence, integrity, energy and performance.

The answer is not to favour older candidates. Let old and new compete. If a younger candidate is better, let that candidate win. If an older candidate is better, why debar that candidate merely because of age? Give the MII the widest pool of talent and let the best person win. That would be a win-win for the candidate, the institution and the market.

Private-sector banks and MIIs are not identical, but both are critical financial institutions. If 70 is compatible with sound governance for the chief executive of a highly regulated private bank, it is reasonable to ask whether a blanket 65-year ceiling for the head of an MII remains justified.

At the same time, technological change cannot be ignored. Artificial intelligence, algorithmic trading, cybersecurity, data analytics and changing investor behaviour require adaptability and fresh thinking. No institution should depend indefinitely on one individual. Leadership renewal and succession planning are essential.

But renewal does not require automatic exclusion. An institution should develop its next generation of leaders while retaining the ability to benefit from an exceptional incumbent where continuity serves the market’s interests.

The more balanced solution may therefore be to retain 65 as the normal retirement age while permitting continuation up to 70 in exceptional cases.

Any extension could require: a fresh assessment by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee; a specific Board recommendation; continuing satisfaction of fit-and-proper requirements; demonstrated performance, competence and fitness; a credible succession plan; and prior regulatory approval.

The extension should be for a defined period and create no automatic right to continue. Such a framework would make 65 a point of heightened accountability rather than automatic retirement.

The writer is former President of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India

Published on September 10, 2026

editorials.title: FCNR(B): Benefits outweigh costs
editorials.passage:
When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) closed its concessional FCNR(B) swap window on August 31, 2026, one month ahead of schedule, it reignited debate over the true cost of the scheme.

Critics have zeroed in on the burden of elevated USD/INR forward premia, which touched more than 1,500 basis points for five-year tenors. Yet, much of the discourse has been speculative, often disconnected from the operational realities. A closer look suggests that while the scheme is not without cost, its benefits outweigh the risks, leaving RBI with a net positive balance sheet impact.

The FCNR(B) swap window was designed to attract foreign currency deposits at concessional swap rates, thereby bolstering India’s external position. In just 85 days, the scheme mobilised an extraordinary $127.2 billion.

Assuming a realistic distribution of deposits, i.e., 40 per cent in three-year tenors, 10 per cent in four-year, and 50 per cent in five-year, the hedging cost and investment yield calculations remain broadly stable even with minor deviations. This assumption reflects depositor preference for longer tenors in a high global interest rate environment, while shorter buckets catered to leveraged positions and immediate obligations.

During the scheme period (June 8-August 31), the average forward premia stood at 2.93 per cent for three-year tenors and 3.23 per cent for five-year tenors.

By contrast, US Treasury yields averaged 4.23 per cent and 4.33 per cent respectively.

RBI, as the central bank, likely secured better than market swap rates, meaning our estimates err on the conservative side. Similarly, while RBI invests primarily in liquid, low-risk assets, not all inflows would be parked in US treasuries, marginally lowering returns. Even so, the numbers are compelling.

Hence, under the best possible scenario, hedging cost was $16.3 billion, while investment income was $22.4 billion, net surplus was $6.1 billion (₹58,372 crore at current exchange rates). [Table 1]

This surplus underscores that the scheme was not a fiscal drag but a calculated intervention yielding tangible gains.

The concessional swaps injected nearly ₹12 trillion of rupee liquidity into the banking system, offering much relief to banks to lend to the productive sectors of the economy, easing the elevated C-D ratio constraint, banks may need couple of quarters to use these surplus funds. However, RBI’s continued forex interventions in selling dollars to control rupee volatility and unwinding its forward book have absorbed much of this surplus.

Indeed, despite $136 billion in foreign capital inflows (including FCNR, ECB, and OFCB), reserves rose by only $59.2 billion as forex kitty grew from 681.6 billion (June 5) to $740.8 (August 28). The rest was offset by intervention and forward settlements. Overnight rates slipped below the repo rate, with call money at 4.95 per cent and TREPS at 4.45 per cent, highlighting the challenge of keeping liquidity within RBI’s comfort zone of 0.5-1 per cent of NDTL. As of mid-August, durable surplus liquidity stood at ₹8.06 lakh crore, forcing RBI into sterilisation operations at a cost.

RBI’s short dollar forward position is currently over $100 billion, with $40 billion maturing within a year. As these positions unwind, liquidity will automatically contract. Meanwhile, surplus liquidity has already nudged banks toward government securities, pushing yields lower and reducing borrowing costs for the government, a secondary benefit of the scheme.

Looking ahead, September and October traditionally strain liquidity. Festive season withdrawals, advance tax payments, credit growth, capex revival, government borrowing, and import payments ahead of Diwali will all absorb liquidity. This seasonal tightening reduces the need for permanent sterilisation mechanisms like the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) of 2004.

Instead, RBI can rely on incremental CRR hikes (as banks benefitted from FCNR swap scheme and the amount is temporarily exempt from CRR and SLR requirement), longer-term VRRRs, and open market operations (OMOs) to manoeuvre liquidity. These tools provide flexibility without locking the system into enduring sterilisation costs.

Even if RBI must sterilise liquidity for up to a year, the costs remain manageable. With surplus liquidity between ₹3-8 trillion and sterilisation rates of 5.3-5.7 per cent (91-day and 364-day T-bills), the one quarter sterilisation cost would range from ₹3,975 crore to ₹10,600 crore and annual sterilisation cost ranges from ₹17,000 crore to ₹45,600 crore.

Against the FCNR(B) surplus of ₹58,372 crore, RBI still nets a positive balance of ₹12,772–₹54,397 crore [Table 2].

The FCNR(B) swap window has achieved its objectives of attracting foreign capital inflows at scale, strengthening the balance of payments, providing banks with liquidity to support credit growth and, reducing government borrowing costs through lower yields.

The beauty of the scheme lies in its cost neutrality across stakeholders, RBI, government, banks, depositors, and ultimately the economy. While sterilisation costs are real, they are temporary and outweighed by the benefits.

In a global environment of tightening liquidity and volatile capital flows, RBI’s decision to front-load inflows through FCNR(B) was both prudent and necessary. The early closure of the window signals confidence. The objectives have been met, reserves strengthened, and liquidity manageable.

The debate over costs should not obscure the larger truth the — FCNR(B) scheme was a net positive intervention, reinforcing India’s financial stability at a critical juncture.

The writer is Visiting Fellow, LSE; and DGM (Economist), State Bank of India. Views expressed are personal

Published on September 10, 2026

editorials.title: Twenty-five years after 9/11: The shadow of distrust
editorials.passage:
There are dates that divide history into a before and an after. September 11, 2001, is one of them. The smoke has disappeared from New York. The towers are gone, and a new skyline has risen in their place. A generation has grown up without a memory of that morning. For them, 9/11 lives in photographs, films, classrooms, and history books. Yet it has not become history in the ordinary sense. Its consequences remain with us. Its deepest legacy may be that the meaning of survival changed. We entered a world in which distrust became almost another name for security.

The terrorists killed nearly 3,000 people and destroyed New York’s skyline. But terrorism has another, more important yet less visible objective: to spread fear. Its weapon is not only the bomb, gun, or hijacked aircraft. It’s the suspicion left behind – of the stranger, the neighbour, the foreigner, often of people who have done nothing wrong, or even of your own shadow.

9/11 was also a spectacular failure of imagination. The world’s most powerful country, with vast military and intelligence resources, failed to imagine an attack of such scale and audacity. In Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s terminology, it had the character of a Black Swan: an event that seemed almost impossible beforehand but, once it happened, changed our understanding of what was possible.

Then came Afghanistan, Iraq, the “War on Terror,” tighter borders, airport security, and expanded surveillance. Yet terrorism didn’t disappear. It changed shape, fragmented, and spread. In trying to defeat it, we sometimes found ourselves fighting the fear it had planted in us. Afghanistan remains the painful example. When American forces finally left in 2021, the scenes from Kabul offered a grim lesson: wars may end on paper while their consequences continue in people’s lives.

But the afterlife of 9/11 is not only geopolitical. It’s personal. TIME’s 25th-anniversary series, How 9/11 Shaped My Life, personalizes the enormity of the event by focusing on the enormity of the event down to individual lives. Colin McShane, for example, was only four and a half when his firefighter father died. He remembers being taken from preschool and watching television, but he was too young to understand what had happened. Only later did the absence of his father become real.

A death happens in an instant. Grief doesn’t. The same is true of those who survived. First responders and others exposed to the dust at Ground Zero have lived with illnesses linked to that day long after the cameras left. The World Trade Center Health Program has cared for more than 150,000 survivors and responders.

Then there was another wound – the social one. After 9/11, a person’s name, face, clothes, or accent could suddenly acquire a political meaning. People often found themselves viewed through suspicion due to their religion or ethnicity. The innocent were made to carry the guilt of the guilty. This is how terror changes a society. It doesn’t merely make people afraid of dying. It can make them afraid of one another.

But there’s another way to respond.
