After the Christchurch mosque attacks in 2019, in which 51 worshippers were killed, New Zealand’s prime minister Jacinda Ardern refused to mention the name of the attacker to deny him the notoriety and fame he sought from his terrorist act. Terror says: “Fear the other.” Ardern’s response was: “They are us.” In Tagore’s iconic play Raktakarabi (Red Oleanders), the wonder woman, Nandini, symbolizes vitality, freedom, and defiance against oppressive systems.

That matters when we consider 9/11. If terrorism seeks to create fear, suspicion, and division, then refusing to surrender to those emotions is itself a form of resistance. We must remember the people who died. But we should also remember the Afghan child whose childhood was shaped by war, the family that lived with suspicion, the first responder who carried Ground Zero in his lungs, and the little boy who grew up without his father.

“Never Forget” must mean more than remembering a terrible morning. It must mean remembering what fear can do to a society – and what humanity can do in response. The towers disappeared. But the shadow remains. Twenty-five years later, the harder question is no longer simply what happened on September 11, 2001? It is: what did we become afterwards?

Perhaps the final measure of survival is whether we resisted the fear that makes us strangers to one another. The date is still being written. Its final meaning may depend not on what the terrorists did to us, but on what we choose to become because of it.

Professor of Statistics, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata

Published on September 10, 2026

editorials.title: Growth gains must widen
editorials.passage:
India’s economy has started the new financial year on a strong note. Real GDP grew 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter, making India once again one of the fastest-growing major economies. Consumption remained reasonably strong, investment picked up and exports also performed better. These are encouraging signs at a time when the global economy remains uncertain. The number deserves to be celebrated. But it also raises a more interesting question: what is driving this growth, and what is it doing to the structure of the Indian economy?

Manufacturing GVA grew 9.2 per cent in the first quarter. Investment in capital goods has also been strong. Yet manufacturing’s share in GDP remains around 16 per cent, roughly where it was a decade ago. In other words, manufacturing is growing, but its weight in the economy has not changed very much. This is not necessarily a contradiction. A sector can grow rapidly without increasing its share if other parts of the economy are also growing. But for India, the distinction matters because manufacturing has traditionally been seen as the bridge between low-productivity work and more productive employment.

There is another interesting part of the story. Corporate profitability has risen sharply in recent years. Strong profits have helped companies repair their balance sheets and should provide resources for fresh investment. The latest GDP numbers suggest that investment is indeed beginning to respond. The real opportunity now lies in connecting these two developments. If higher corporate profits lead to more investment, and investment creates larger manufacturing ecosystems, supply chains and new businesses, the benefits can spread much beyond the large companies at the top. That is when growth starts changing the structure of the economy.

This matters particularly for India’s young population. Urban youth unemployment remains high, at around 18 per cent. The problem is not simply the absence of jobs. It is also the difficulty of creating enough productive jobs for young people entering the labour market every year. India therefore faces an unusual situation. It has relatively strong economic growth, rising investment and increasingly profitable companies, but the transition towards a more employment-intensive economy remains incomplete.

There is, however, good reason to be optimistic. The foundations are considerably stronger today than they were a decade ago. India’s physical infrastructure has improved, digital connectivity has expanded, domestic companies have become more competitive and global firms are looking at India as an alternative production base. The recent increase in investment suggests that some of these changes are beginning to translate into actual economic activity.

A large factory can create thousands of jobs. But the bigger impact comes when it also creates demand for hundreds of smaller suppliers, transport operators, technicians, designers and service providers. A successful manufacturing ecosystem can generate opportunities well beyond the factory gate.

India does not have a growth problem in the conventional sense. It has a conversion problem: converting growth into productive employment, investment into wider industrial capacity, and India’s large domestic market into globally competitive businesses. In this context, the 7.8 per cent growth rate gives us reason for confidence. The relatively modest change in manufacturing’s share and the continuing challenge of youth employment tell us that there is still considerable ground to cover. That is not a pessimistic conclusion. In fact, it is an opportunity. The next achievement would be to ensure that this growth changes the lives of a much larger number of people — not only through higher incomes, but through better jobs, more productive firms and greater economic mobility.

The writer is with NCAER, New Delhi. Views are personal

Published on September 10, 2026

editorials.title: Agentic AI changes the business services playbook
editorials.passage: By Rohit Puri, Business process services (BPS) are entering a new phase of evolution. Enterprises today are moving away from traditional robotic process automation (RPA) and investing in autonomous AI agents capable of analysing data, decision-making and execute actions across business functions. The move towards agentic BPS has the potential to fundamentally reshape how organisations operate at scale. As AI adoption accelerates, these systems are transforming from being simple action assistants to autonomous, decision-making partners. As per Gartner, by 2028, at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously by agentic AI. It also reports that 33% of enterprise software applications will include agentic capabilities, which is currently less than 1%. In enterprise context, agentic systems today represent a cultural shift by coordinating multi-stage workflows, collaborating across business functions, learning from feedback and adapting their decisions based on outcomes. The AI systems are increasingly being deployed in environments like cloud operations and business services. The rise of agentic AI highlights risks like access control, regulatory exposure and auditability – underscoring the importance of human oversight and governance. ALSO READBoardroom’s next governance challenge: AI agents Why closed-loop model is essential A key design principle emerging from enterprise AI implementation is the use of closed-loop operating models. These models feature two layers which integrate intelligence, insight, orchestration and oversight allowing organisations to not only deploy agentic AI responsibly but also improve continuously with feedback. The first step is the intelligence layer (Presto) which analyses enterprise data, workflow patterns and performance metrics to identify opportunities for automation while also flagging areas of risk. With constant monitoring of autonomous agents, this layer can reveal inefficiencies, deviations from normal operation and potential compliance gaps. This helps enterprises build transparency in agentic AI operations, improving its trustworthiness and aiding in successful adoption. Post analysis comes the orchestration layer (DICE), which governs the lifecycle of these agentic systems. The second layer allows organisations to embed the guardrails, policies and audit capabilities directly into the design and deployment of autonomous agents – making their actions visible and adjustable with evolving conditions. Both layers work together to create a feedback-driven governance loop, strengthening both performance and control over time. The model comes across as a powerful tool with continuous learning and refinement, while also being rooted in operational transparency.  Agentic business process services - The next frontier As organisations today move away from RPAs towards agentic AI, a parallel shift is underway towards services-as-software (SaS), a dashboard-like platform that is modular, scalable and subscription-based, delivering packaged, outcome-focussed capabilities ready to plug-in and use. At the core of this is agentic business process as a service (BPaaS) which involves AI agents that autonomously run entire business process from start to finish. Pairing this system with the closed-loop model, ensures that while the process become autonomous, they remain transparent, auditable and aligned to business objectives. This evolution enables business agility and faster time-to-value, allowing organisation leaders to focus on business priorities, while the AI agents take care of the execution. ALSO READGoogle report warns of AI-powered cyberattacks becoming more autonomous Agentic AI is already reshaping how business process services work across sectors: Contact centres use AI agents to autonomously summarise calls and resolve issues, escalating to human judgement only when necessary. Insurance providers can run real-time eligibility checks, asses claims and initial payouts without any human touchpoints. AI agents in finance reconcile accounts, flag anomalies and keep a perfect audit trail. Human resource teams can use AI agents to automate onboarding, resume screening and other functions. Governance built in, not retrofitted Agentic AI differs from traditional automation by not following pre-defined rules, but rather acting autonomously by monitoring context, adapting to changing conditions and achieve outcomes. This is one of the clearest lessons for enterprise AI adoption that governance must be baked into every layer of the agentic system design and cannot be a retrofit post deployment. Governance frameworks focus on transparency, auditability and ethical safeguards. These frameworks aim to deliver trusted AI services, aligning with legal and societal norms and serve as a critical component for responsibly scaling autonomous agents. By embedding policy-based guardrails, role-based permissions and real-time controls, enterprises can scale autonomy without amplifying risks. Human oversight remains essential Despite rapid advances in autonomy, AI won’t replace humans but rather aid in amplifying the speed and scale of decision-making. Enterprises consistently indicate that human oversight plays a crucial role in ensuring trust and sustainability of fully autonomous operations. Human oversight plays a key role in defining strategic intent by setting goals, risk tolerance and ethical boundaries; providing judgement by reviewing highlighted edge-case errors before taking further action; ensure accountability and responsibility of decisions made that satisfy governance frameworks. Human oversight not only acts as a safety measure, but as a competitive advantage. This “humans in-the-loop” hybrid model combines the speed and scale of autonomous agents with the judgement and contextual awareness of human stakeholders, preserving trust, safety and quality. Scaling autonomy with trust Agentic BPS isn’t just a technology upgrade, but rather an operating model shift. With human oversight, closed-loop models continuously identify opportunities and orchestrate agents responsibly achieving speed without chaos, scale without risk amplification and innovate without eroding trust. In a world where autonomous AI agents become embedded into core business processes, its future belongs to organisations which place human oversight at the centre of intelligent operations. The writer is global head, Business Process Services, NTT Data. Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author’s own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: Trump’s repeated threats to ‘wipe out’ Iran are normalizing mass violence
editorials.passage:
A s the US and Iran fought around the strait of Hormuz last week, Donald Trump issued one of his typical threats. In an interview with a Fox News correspondent, Trump said Iran would be “totally wiped out as a country” if it retaliated for the latest wave of US air strikes.

That threat by the US president to wipe out another country generated few headlines , even during a relatively slow news week by Trump administration standards.

Trump has delivered this kind of warning so frequently over the past six months of his war against Iran that it hardly registers anymore. But it’s important not to normalize Trump’s threats, which are usually accompanied by promises to devastate Iran’s infrastructure – vowing to destroy bridges and power plants. Those kinds of attacks would constitute war crimes under international law.

The president’s repeated vows to obliterate Iran are usually written off by other western leaders and the news media as typical of Trump’s bravado and unpredictability, but they have real-world consequences. By treating Trump’s rhetoric as normal, US and western societies are becoming more desensitized to the idea of large-scale violence – including the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure – as a legitimate kind of warfare. And of course, Israel’s war on Gaza has inured many in the western world to wholesale atrocities , including intense aerial bombardment that leads to massive civilian casualties and displacement.

Trump set the stage for apocalyptic threats against Iran weeks into the war, when it became clear that the US would not achieve the quick military victory he was hoping for. On 7 April, as he vacillated between agreeing to a ceasefire and ordering even more intense bombing, Trump ominously declared in a social media post : “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.”

In the days leading up to that statement, Trump had issued a series of warnings that the US would destroy Iran’s infrastructure unless it reopened the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies flowed before Tehran effectively shut the waterway at the start of the war. On 1 April, in a primetime address from the White House, Trump threatened to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages, where they belong”. On 6 April, Trump claimed that Iran “could be taken out in one night” and said the US had a plan to destroy every bridge and power plant in the country, leaving that infrastructure “burning, exploding, and never to be used again” – a statement announcing his intention to commit war crimes.

Trump set a deadline of 8 pm ET on 7 April for Iranian leaders to comply with his demands. As that deadline neared, Trump shared his now infamous post on his Truth Social network that promised to erase Iran’s civilization. That threat to carry out large-scale war crimes against a country of 90 million people prompted outrage around the world, with condemnation from the UN secretary general and the pope. Some human rights experts argued that Trump’s statement may constitute a threat to commit genocide, which is defined by the UN’s Genocide Convention as acts committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group”.

Shortly before Trump’s deadline expired, Pakistan’s prime minister announced that the US and Iran had agreed to an immediate ceasefire. But Trump never apologized or retracted his statement. And why should he feel any pressure to do so, despite the momentary outrage his words caused? In today’s world, there are no consequences for threatening – or carrying out – a genocide.

Trump’s threat to obliterate Iran is partly a manifestation of a new international order that emerged over the past three years, as the US supplied billions of dollars in weapons and protected Israel as it carried out a genocidal war in Gaza. In his second term, Trump has behaved more erratically and like an autocrat drunk with power. But he has also taken advantage of a nascent global order, in which western leaders destroyed decades of international norms and the façade of rule of law – all to enable Israel to continue its bloodshed in Gaza, and more recently, in Lebanon .

As they did with Gaza, most western powers and leaders have become numb to the loss and suffering of Palestinians, Iranians, Lebanese and others in the Middle East. And as long as this numbness and impunity continue, it will become normal for the US president to threaten whole-scale destruction of societies and civilizations, as Trump has done in Iran.

While Trump can be dismissed as an unpredictable, or even irrational, world leader who scorns global institutions and norms – the epitome of the “madman theory” of US foreign policy – his predecessor Joe Biden helped paved the way for the current age of impunity we’re living in. Biden, along with other western leaders who provided unwavering support to Israel after the Hamas attacks in October 2023, defied and weakened international law in order to shield Israel long before Trump returned to office in early 2025.

For 15 months, the Biden administration undermined global institutions – including the international court of justice (ICJ) and the international criminal court (ICC) – to help Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, avoid facing consequences for their war crimes in Gaza. Biden and other western leaders rendered international law meaningless after their inaction and obstruction in Gaza – and it was only a matter of time before Trump abandoned any pretense of lofty rhetoric about human rights and rule of law. Trump prefers to flaunt American military power and his ability to inflict massive destruction on US enemies.

The normalization of Israel’s atrocities in Gaza has rippled across the world, including the expanding regional war that engulfed Iran and the US. It has also diluted international outrage at Trump’s repeated threats to destroy Iran, even within a period of months. While Trump’s apocalyptic warning in April that “a whole civilization will die” prompted global condemnation, his subsequent rhetoric has barely registered.

In July, Trump claimed that the US would bomb one Iranian bridge or power plant in retaliation for each time Iran fired at a ship in the strait of Hormuz. That kind of retaliation against civilian targets would be a war crime, but Trump has made such threats seem mundane and a normal part of warfare. At the very least, Americans and the rest of the world should call him out on it.

Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

editorials.title: Is Burnham trying to appease Trump? Or Reform? What other reason is there for these North Sea oil plans?
editorials.passage:
P inch yourself, it’s happening again. Here is a Labour government spending a vast amount of political capital to earn tiny material gains while risking huge political losses. It occurred repeatedly under Keir Starmer, and now – with the impending decision to approve further gas and oil drilling in the North Sea – it is happening under Andy Burnham. You rack your brains to explain it, but no rational explanation comes.

Burnham is studiously cryptic about his reasons. His clearest statement to date goes as follows: “There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.” Does he mean that oil and gas workers are struggling? If so, this decision will be of little use to them. The Jackdaw gasfield, likely to be approved this week, will generate a grand total of 27 direct full-time jobs . The Rosebank oilfield, whose approval is likely to follow soon, will support 450 UK-based jobs during its lifetime. Yet the UK’s net zero economy directly employs 300,000 people , and a further 400,000 jobs are planned. The rest of the green economy employs more than 600,000 . A just transition for fossil fuel workers, securing jobs in the green economy, is better for everyone.

Or does he mean energy consumers are struggling? The gas in the Jackdaw field will make a tiny contribution to our supply and no significant difference to either our energy bills or our energy security . Switching to renewables makes us far better off in both respects. Any oil produced by the Rosebank field is unlikely to be refined in Britain , as we no longer possess much capacity for handling oil of that kind. And as for the national accounts, a recent estimate suggests that the climate damage caused by the fields’ extra emissions would outweigh any economic benefits several times over.

In fact, the two greatest threats to the global economy might now be climate breakdown, which, as a wide range of economists and eminent organisations forecast, threatens comprehensive economic collapse , and the AI bubble, which the governor of the Bank of England warns could burst with dire consequences. Then people will really be struggling. Yet our government and others cheerfully accelerate both forces – claiming, as ever, that the industries driving them will unleash “growth”. Growth in home repossessions, perhaps.

While the small amount of fossil fuel these two fields will produce allows politicians to argue that their climate impacts can be ignored, the diplomatic implications are considerable. The only chance of preventing climate catastrophe is international agreement based on mutual trust. To its credit, the UK – while falling short of what many of us would like to see – has been a leader in these efforts. But when our government refuses to leave fossil fuels in the ground, its credibility diminishes – leaving its negotiating position weakened .

Burnham might believe this decision will get Reform UK and the Conservatives off his back. Of course it won’t. He might imagine it will appease Donald Trump , but you can’t appease Trump. Whatever you give him, he will always want more.

As for the political implications, here the disparity between gain and pain becomes truly enormous. The approval of these fields is a defining issue for many Labour MPs and the voters they fear they might lose. The policy could scarcely be better designed to give the final push to voters who are minded – after so many disappointments since 2024 – to abandon Labour for a progressive alternative.

If Zack Polanski, the Green party leader for England and Wales, wins the seat Keir Starmer has just vacated , this could be a major reason why. Burnham’s North Sea policy is the kind of battle Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney would have urged him to wage – let’s stick it to the Labour left , mwahaha – which is a major reason why Starmer is no longer prime minister.

Few in power seem to understand the fire they are playing with. Last week, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, appeared to acknowledge that we face the risk of potentially catastrophic environmental breakdown and urged us to store some extra food in our homes. The way she put it suggested that either she hasn’t grasped the magnitude of what we face, or she is trivialising the issue: “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t.”

Right. So let’s imagine one of several possible disasters some of us have long been warning of arrives. As a result of harvest failures caused by climate breakdown, severe transport disruptions or – and this now looks alarmingly plausible – sudden systemic collapse in the food sector, the supermarket shelves empty, more or less overnight. We know that the UK government refuses , without explanation, to maintain strategic food reserves. So there are no government supplies, either. As our beans and crackers run out, the emergency services visit all 29 million of our homes. With what? Tea and sympathy? Sorry, no tea. Another slice of sympathy?

Certainly, those of us who have the money and capacity to store food should do so : after all, no one else has our backs. But the idea that such individuated solutions would be any use in the face of a societal catastrophe is neoliberal nonsense. As always, it is the poor and excluded, with neither the cash nor the space to lay down significant supplies, who will be hit first and worst. Social breakdown would happen in days. The UK government, then, is being serious about neither the measures required to prevent climate catastrophe nor the measures required to survive it.

The sense in almost every nation is of governments failing to take seriously the most serious of issues, while spending immense political resources on topics that scarcely affect our welfare (such as a few thousand people crossing the Channel in small boats). Or even – as is the case with North Sea oil and gas – using their scarce political capital to make things worse for everyone, including themselves.

Our government is not a doomsday cult like the Trump government, creepily fascinated by the “end times”, as the US vice-president seems to be . But in terms of outcome, is there much difference?

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity
editorials.passage:
N ine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, was assassinated by a car bomb outside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder.

Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association.

We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law.

We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it.

The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure.

But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed.

Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, he gave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma , the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted he passed confidential information about the police investigation to Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma.

But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends.

The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle.

Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law.

The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating.

There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings.

Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta.

Malta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across the European Union . Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union.

This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem.

On Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom.

The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary.

Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further.

Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta.

Europe owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability.

The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else.

Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again.

Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in Malta

editorials.title: Ridiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?
editorials.passage:
A s welcome-back-to-Britain gestures go, the lord chamberlain’s letter , sent on behalf of King Charles on Monday to remind Harry, Meghan and everyone watching that they’re still “private citizens”, was so perfect as to restore me to monarchism. After six years in the wilderness, what greater comfort for Prince Harry than to find himself, once again, in the familiar waters of this country’s passive aggression, being attacked by his father via the merciless phrase “fully respected”, and provoking from the prince a coded up-yours in the form of his publicly stated “surprise”.

Well, it’s up there with better cheese, bread and the NHS, isn’t it?! Even the most Eurocentric American can’t match us for this kind of subtextual bare-knuckle fight. Before we get into what else the returnees may be enjoying this month, let’s fully excavate the letter’s encrypted hostility. First, the king’s repeated use of the words “personal” and “private” – as in “the charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” – is so intense, so heavy handed, as to go beyond merely calling his younger son a civilian and come perilously close to the ultimate insult, “middle class”.

Second, this: “in short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”. As we know, opening a sentence with “in short” is an absolute middle finger of a move, up there for officiousness with “furthermore”, “with respect”, “to be clear” and “I think you’ll find”. Elsewhere in that sentence, roping together the words “commercial” and “charitable”, is, I would suggest, a deliberate tactic to insinuate that the former (grubby little money-makers!) undermines the integrity of the latter (charitable, my arse!) and suggest that the Sussexes are just in it for themselves.

And finally: the absolute shellacking of the letter’s dismount, in which the king writes: “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”

Or in layperson’s language: “haha, you’re not royal any more, nothing in your status warrants the sustained use of capital letters or a requirement for history to remember you. We’re not giving you any money because you’ve brought this on yourselves and ps, your invocation of privacy, post the publication of your memoir and your sit-down with Oprah, is an absolute joke we couldn’t be enjoying more. See ya.” God the seething, green bile acidity of the phrase “as they would wish”! Bravo, sir! Absolutely gold standard! Poor Harry must be reeling, even as he relaxes into the warm gust of air in which he was raised. (Meghan, one assumes, is largely oblivious to just how devastating all of this is and may have found the letter merely a touch snotty.)

For the formerly royal couple, we must assume that any upset caused by the tone of this letter – and allowing for the prince’s bone-deep recognition and masochistic enjoyment of what might otherwise be an upsetting exchange – is offset by the many advantages they will enjoy now they’re back in the old country. Rolling green hills are obviously a thing of the past; the Cotswolds are as brown as southern California right now. But the prince may find comfort in the small-scale landscape, the patchwork of fields and hedgerows, the tiny lanes like crooked elbows, jammed up with tractors and alive with tiny brown birds, that large-scale farming in the US doesn’t do.

I mentioned the cheese and the bread, infinitely superior to the rubbery and sugary American equivalents, and I’d add English strawberries to that, even this late in the season. Perhaps Harry will be reunited with some of his old wardrobe favourites, too. It’s never wax jacket season in Montecito, where an extreme heat warning is in place; meanwhile, the whole of this country is down on all fours excavating its woolly jumpers from under the bed. (Don’t tell me the words “woolly jumper” won’t soothe Harry after enforced wearing of sweaters and hoodies.) For Meghan, these consolations will be alien, but perhaps, before it starts to enrage her, she can find comfort in this country’s relative slowness, its high tolerance for dishevelment and appreciation for sarcasm – failing which, there’s always the pub.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Australia has recognised the state of Palestine. Now we must act to protect what settler terrorism is tearing to shreds
editorials.passage:
R oughly 5,900 Palestinians have been completely or partially displaced by settler violence since January 2023, along with 32,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from their homes in West Bank refugee camps last year.

The scale of this prompted Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, someone who spent his life fighting for Israel , and who recently visited the occupied West Bank, to remark: “This, what the settlers are doing here, is the real threat to Israel. This is more concerning to me than Iran, Gaza or Lebanon.”

The former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general Ephraim Sneh said: “This is ethnic cleansing, to put it simply.” Retired air force general Asaf Agmon declared: “Once a society behaves this way – that society is doomed.”

One of our most significant allies believes what’s happening in the West Bank is wrong.

The UK Labour government, led by new prime minister Andy Burnham, decided enough was enough. They took action, targeting illegal settlements and settlement expansion through banning imports.

Oddly, even before the UK formally announced their moves, our own government declared we wouldn’t embrace the same measures.

I’d be misleading the parliament if I was to say I wasn’t disappointed.

To justify this decision, it was said: “We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis.”

By way of contrast, it’s worth noting Australia has imposed 1,800 sanctions and strict tariffs on Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, which has seen the total value of Australia’s imports from Russia drop by around 99%.

And it would sound quite odd for us to say we wouldn’t impose sanctions on Russia because of the impact on Australian businesses or Ukrainians or Russians.

We took action knowing it would have an impact, precisely because we wanted it to lead to change.

Additionally we’ve pointed out regularly that we – as an individual nation – couldn’t possibly act on our own regarding what’s happening in the West Bank or Gaza .

Yet many Australians would then question why we wouldn’t act when we had a chance to do so in concert with many like-minded nations.

But let me come back to the issue of impacts. Let’s look at this another way.

It was former prime minister Bob Hawke who dedicated so much of himself, in such a principled and unyielding way, to ending apartheid in South Africa.

As a prime minister he pushed on the world stage for comprehensive financial sanctions against South Africa, measures that were so tough, the former foreign minister Gareth Evans said they were “profoundly practically important in their economic, and ultimately, endgame political impact.”

Now, imagine telling Bob Hawke not to impose bans or measures on South Africa because it would affect Australian businesses or the very South Africans resisting apartheid?

Bob Hawke championed a cause that forms an important part of Labor history.

Likewise prime minister Anthony Albanese has led a government that can justifiably be proud to be part of history it has written: the first ever Australian government to recognise the state of Palestine .

But having stated the ambition, we must act to protect it.

Because settler terrorism is tearing to shreds our ambition to see a state of Palestine – and we cannot sticky tape that back together with yet another statement.

It’s why I have urged regularly – before and after our ALP national conference – the need for concrete action.

Because the Netanyahu government will simply ride out the flurry of statements that our country or other nations issue.

And we should recognise the expectations of so many Australians, who want to see action taken to see the end of suffering for innocent Palestinians.

Among those Australians are many members of our own party, who joined driven by a sense of purpose, a sense of social justice. Who believe that that commitment to social justice simply does not end at our own borders.

In fact I’m reminded of the words of Ben Chifley in 1949: “We have a great objective – the light on the hill – which we aim to reach by working the betterment of mankind not only here but anywhere we may give a helping hand.”

Nearly a dozen other nations agreed to join the UK in its stand this week.

The only government to enthusiastically support our government’s decision not to join the UK and other nations to take a stand on settler terrorism in West Bank? The Netanyahu government.

Ed Husic is the federal Labor MP for Chifley in western Sydney. This is an abridged version of his speech to parliament on Thursday

editorials.title: My friend Blanche d’Alpuget often spoke to me about death. She once likened it to ‘untying a million little knots’
editorials.passage:
T hirty-six hours before Blanche took her last breath , I negotiated the plastic tubes and mask she wore over a still beautiful face and gave her one final kiss. I wasn’t sure, then, if it was a goodbye but I knew it would be close.

Was she really, as the Sydney Morning Herald described her in an appreciation for Hazel Hawke, just “some lipsticked wraith”, a prowling blonde, the avatar for the other woman?

It was a cruel fate for a woman who was so pivotal in Australian literature and politics. It wasn’t easy to disrupt Blanche but the breadth of animosity she encountered after her affair with Bob Hawke became public in late 1994 was like nothing she’d ever experienced.

About 30 years after she was photographed with Hawke at Sir Richard Kirby’s holiday house, she told me: “I was very shocked and distressed by the trolling and abuse … as opposed to simple literary criticism. I developed a great contempt, distrust and loathing of journalists.”

Blanche first blew into my orbit in a tornado of Doris Day hair and Sophia Loren lips in the winter of 2016, looking at least a decade younger than her 72 years, as I pursued her husband for my first book, Wednesdays with Bob . Her silk cravat and wide black sunglasses touched on the side with gold detail delivered a 70s movie-star sheen.

As she turned the corner into 80, the age when she presumed her face would suddenly collapse, as her mother’s did, and she would become a crone, I was struck by this realisation: Australia would never know the story of this woman, whose own trajectory was as compelling as that of the man whose life would come to define her.

Born the daughter of one of Australia’s great journalists, Blanche moved to Jakarta at 22 with her first husband, Tony Pratt, where she had a front-row seat as Indonesia struggled with the bloodletting of 1965. She challenged the bolted-on moral codes of the time with her fearless writing, and her bestselling biography of Hawke, published in 1982, helped propel him into the prime ministership and thus helped change Australian politics for ever. She was still writing and living life to the full while many others of her vintage were staggering, zombie-like, along the fluorescent-lit corridors of a nursing home.

And so, at the suggestion of our mutual agent, Jeanne Ryckmans, a book deal was sought and made.

If Wednesdays were spent with her husband, Fridays would be with Blanche. Over the course of late 2023 and through 2024, we lunched, talked, messaged and flirted.

Over several lunches, our talks had drifted to the topic of dying. It seemed, then, that everyone was dropping like flies.

Death and the process of dying interested her deeply. She believed death was like walking through a fiery door but that the pain was only temporary.

Blanche had seen up close what it’s like to die. She had nursed her mother through her final hours, remaining awake for days, and did an all-nighter alongside Hawke on his final day.

She likened dying to “untying a million little knots”.

“The soul wants to be released, but it’s held in by the body very, very strongly, and it’s an enormous effort to untie all of those knots,” she said.

Regarding her final wishes, she said that her headstone was already in place next to Hawke’s at the Macquarie Park Cemetery and Crematorium in Sydney’s North Ryde.

Her coffin, she told me, must be red on the inside and blue and white on the exterior. The blue represented the sky, red the colour of life and white the spirit.

Blanche wanted a band to play When the Saints Go Marching In.

“The more humans there are, the more love there is,” Blanche liked to say.

“Love is, I believe, what distinguishes humans from the rest of the animal world or creation. Love that extends beyond one’s family and friends, beyond the blood bonds of tribe and race, to all other humans and to the rest of creation.”

Derek Rielly is the author of Fridays with Blanche . His previous books are Wednesdays with Bob, a biography of the former prime minister Bob Hawke, and Gulpilil, a biography of the Australian actor and dancer David Gulpilil

editorials.title: The war in the Gulf will have to end in compromise
editorials.passage:
The current Gulf war does not look like other wars. Conflicts, whether short or prolonged, usually end in one of two ways. Either one side achieves a decisive victory over the other, typically followed by the signing of a surrender agreement and the imposition of the victor’s terms on the defeated party, as happened in the first and second world wars, both of which ended in Allied victory. Or such wars end in a settlement based on the principle of “no victor and no vanquished”, with each side throwing the full extent of its military capabilities into battle against the other. Both sides are exhausted without either achieving a decisive result, at which point they move to end the fighting and reach a settlement that takes their interests into account. The war then ends almost as though it had never begun, apart from the human and material losses it caused.

One example is the Iran-Iraq war, which lasted eight years without either Iran or Iraq achieving its objectives. Iraq did not liberate Arabistan, and Iran did not succeed in overthrowing Iraq’s Baath Party regime.

Looking at America’s modern wars, the truth is that it has not won any of them. It may not have been defeated, but it did not achieve the objectives for which those wars were fought. The image of the helicopter evacuations from Saigon remains vivid, as does the historic scene at Kabul airport, when America’s allies clung desperately to a lifeline, to no avail.

In the Vietnam War, the Americans lost nearly 60,000 military personnel. The result was an agreement in Paris to end the war and provide the United States with a way out, amid a clear Vietnamese victory. The Americans withdrew from Vietnam and the country was unified on Vietnamese terms.

The same was true of the US war in Afghanistan. Thousands of tonnes of bombs were dropped on the country, only for the United States to withdraw suddenly and chaotically, in scenes that resembled an escape from disaster. Then there was the US invasion of Iraq, where the war seemed almost to have been fought on Iran’s behalf. What Tehran had been unable to achieve during the eight-year war, America achieved for it by handing Iraq over to Iran. America may lose wars, but it does not learn from them before starting another.

Today, the current Gulf war is strange and falls outside both of these familiar patterns. Last year, we were surprised by a US-Israeli war on Iran that lasted a little less than two weeks, with the aim of eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme. Yet it suddenly stopped. US warships departed, and Israeli aircraft left the skies above Tehran without dropping their payloads, following a decision by the US president. Both sides claimed victory, despite the fact that the objective of the war had not been achieved.

Things remained unchanged for months before the war suddenly resumed. At the time, the Americans and Iranians were engaged in negotiations mediated by Oman, and talks between the parties were supposed to resume just one day after the start of massive military operations: relentless bombardment from US warships and Israeli aircraft flying around the clock over Iranian cities.

The second surprise was that this war, too, stopped without warning, ushering in a period of threats that fighting would resume: US and Israeli threats met by Iranian threats, and an intermittent war in which an American strike is answered by an Iranian one, and so on. Israel, the occupying state, has meanwhile been kept out of this contest of wills.

This, then, is not a war like other wars. It resembles a cockfight. Nor is it being fought according to the principle of “no victor and no vanquished”. Both sides continue to claim that they possess the will and the ability to fight.

On the battlefield, every American strike is met by an Iranian strike, even if the Iranian response has less impact. But this means that the Iranians have not surrendered, that their resolve has not weakened and that they still retain a relative capacity to confront their adversary.

Turning to President Trump’s decision to maintain the blockade on Iran and tighten the economic sanctions he has described as devastating and unprecedented, it is worth remembering that sanctions have been imposed on Iran for more than 40 years.

This invites comparison with the sanctions and blockade imposed on Iraq after its invasion of Kuwait, which led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands amid shortages of food and medicine and impoverished Iraqis to the point that they sold their most valuable possessions simply to meet the costs of everyday life.

The blockade and sanctions therefore had an enormous impact on the lives of Iraqis. But is Iran’s situation comparable with Iraq’s? I believe it is entirely different, and the comparison is inaccurate. Iran is several times the size of Iraq. Iraq was surrounded by countries hostile to its political regime, including Iran and Syria. Its only lifeline was Jordan, which was itself constrained at the port of Aqaba to prevent any breach of the blockade.

Iran’s situation is different. It has extensive borders with several countries, including Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Iraq. There is no clear hostility between Iran and these states that would lead them to tighten the blockade or adhere rigidly to US sanctions. Iraq, in fact, amounts to an open border through which Iran can obtain whatever it needs.

More importantly still, Iran has a coastline of roughly 700 kilometres on the Caspian Sea, which opens onto several countries, most notably Russia, which shares the sea with Iran and maintains good relations with Tehran. For this reason, I do not believe that the blockade and sanctions, however severe they become, will force the Iranians to back down or surrender.

In my view, if the Iranians were given a choice between surrender and fighting another war, they might choose war. They still appear to possess a degree of strength and perhaps the ability to rebuild their capabilities as well.

In conclusion, the objectives behind this US-Israeli war on Iran were to end Iran’s nuclear programme, eliminate its missile system or at least limit its range, and overthrow the regime. None of these three objectives has been achieved. It is true that the supreme leader and many Iranian leaders have been killed, that large parts of the country’s infrastructure have been destroyed and that Iran’s military capabilities have been weakened. Despite all this, the current Iranian leadership has become more hardline than its predecessors.

What is striking is the issue of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. It was not a direct cause of the outbreak of war, but it has become one of its consequences. It is almost as though the US-Israeli objectives of the war had been achieved, even though they have not. Restoring freedom of navigation through the strait has now become the urgent priority, in order to prevent a global rise in oil prices and avert a worldwide recession and financial and economic crisis. As a result, all efforts are now focused on this issue, while discussion of the original reasons for the war has receded.

Finally, mediation efforts must intensify, with other influential powers such as Europe and China joining the commendable efforts already being made by Pakistan, Oman and Qatar. Their involvement could give mediation greater weight, perhaps influencing the parties to the conflict and bringing them towards a compromise that safeguards everyone’s interests, ensures the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, spares the world a financial and economic crisis, and protects Arab states from bombardment and violations of their security and national sovereignty, even though they are not parties to this war.
