editorials.title: Behind deaths of Adivasi children in Balaghat: appalling vaccination levels, widespread hunger
editorials.passage:
In June, one-year-old Sahil caught a fever and developed a rash all over his body. A month later, he was dead, mostly likely from a measles-malaria outbreak that ripped through Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district.

Sahil’s 12-year-old sister Lamnin fell ill with similar symptoms and died a day later at their home in Bondari village.

As Scroll reported in the first part of this series, at least 25 children from the Baiga and Gond tribes have died since May in this remote Adivasi habitation in Madhya Pradesh. For two months, the outbreak went undetected because of the complete absence of a healthcare system in the area.

Measles is a disease that can be prevented through vaccination. India added the measles vaccine to its universal immunisation programme in 1985.

But four decades later, in the villages of Balaghat, we found that immunisation drives against measles existed only on paper.

Sahil’s father Samaroo Dhurwey said that neither Sahil nor Lamlin had been vaccinated against measles.

Dhurwey told Scroll that none of his seven children had ever been immunised against any disease. His eldest daughter is married, and the youngest is five years old.

But the records maintained in the Kohnimod anganwadi in Bondari village show that Sahil last received one dose of the measles vaccine on April 21 this year, along with a Vitamin A injection and the pneumococcal vaccine.

After the death of two of his children, Dhurwey alleged that he was asked by a local health worker to say that both had been vaccinated. “ Par mein jhoot kyu bolu,” he said. “But why should I lie?”

When we spoke to Lalita Dhurwey, the anganwadi worker, she said she had joined the post in May and did not know about the entry against Sahil’s name. However, she admitted the health department had not carried out any vaccination rounds since she began work.

Kapil Yadav, a teacher at a primary school that stands next to the anganwadi, told Scroll that for months he “kept insisting” that the health department vaccinate the schoolchildren”.

“But the anganwadi or health department did not carry out routine immunisation properly here,” he said.

Experts Scroll spoke to said the low levels of vaccination allowed the measles virus to spread like wildfire in the region. In the Birsa block of Balaghat, which saw many of the deaths, there has been no recorded measles outbreak in the last two decades.

That’s not all. As Scroll found out, the outbreak became deadlier for the children because many of them were malnourished. Moreover, the government’s take-home rations for children aged under six years had recently stopped, compounding the crisis.

Three weeks after Sahil and Lamnin’s deaths, three-year-old Priti died in the neighbouring village of Kundekasa.

She had symptoms similar to the other deceased children – high fever, rashes on her body and whitish spots in the mouth, which were suggestive of a measles infection.

The register kept at the local anganwadi shows that Priti received her first dose of measles vaccine in December 2023.

The first dose of the vaccine is given to babies between the age of nine and twelve months and the second dose at 16-24 months.

She was one of the lucky few. The vaccination register listed 15 children – and 11 had missed their first measles shot.

Priti missed her second dose, which can affect a child’s long-term immunity against the virus.

She died on July 22. The cause of her death is “unknown”.

Soon after her death, the administration began mass surveillance in villages in the Birsa block. Until then, the health department was unaware of a measles outbreak.

In 2025, the health ministry set a target for elimination of measles by 2026 through 100% immunisation. India, however, has not met that deadline. We recorded 26,332 measles cases in the first half of 2026. Before this, India missed deadlines to eliminate measles in 2015, 2020 and 2023.

Data from the ministry shows that till 2025, 92.2% of children in India received both doses against the measles virus.

In Balaghat, the coverage is much lower. According to the latest round of National Family Health Survey, 81.3% children have received both the measles shots.

In Birsa, where the outbreak began, the Adivasi villages have even lower vaccination coverage. According to a team from the World Health Organisation that surveyed 177 children in the Birsa block this August, 80% had received their first measles vaccine and 70% their second.

But our investigation revealed that vaccination coverage was far worse than those figures suggest.

We visited families of seven deceased children to check their vaccination status. Parents of six children said they had never been inoculated against any disease. One parent said her child had been administered at least two vaccines, but was not sure for which disease.

Congress MLA Sanjay Uikey asserted that “none of the deceased children were fully vaccinated against measles”. Scroll could not verify this claim.

In Bondari village, Sukhwati bai, a helper at the local anganwadi, claimed parents refuse immunisation even if there is a camp held. Sukhwati herself did not get her eight children vaccinated. Her son Roop Lal, aged 16, died on August 10.

But Budhan Singh who lives in the same village said nobody from the health department held regular camps or visited them to explain the need for vaccines and their benefits. Singh’s four children have not received any vaccine, he claimed. “The health workers are coming now after all these deaths,” he said.

Data from the health department shows that officials conducted a ‘catch-up’ round of measles vaccination – administering 10,481 doses till August 28 – after the outbreak was discovered.

The vaccination officer, Dr Paresh Uplap, was removed from his post as the deaths were discovered. He was also removed from the post of the chief medical health officer in Balaghat.

Uplap admitted that “measles vaccination coverage could improve in Birsa” but maintained that measles alone did not kill at this scale. “The high number of deaths that happened here were because these children had other health issues,” he said.

Balaghat is a malaria-endemic zone.

In 2024, the containment zone of 40 villages where the outbreak took a toll recorded 697 malaria cases. In 2025, there were 492 cases.

Strikingly, this year in just one month, from July end to August end, the villages recorded 404 malaria cases.

Two senior officials from the Balaghat health department told Scroll they believe there has been “massive under-reporting in malaria cases” over the past few years. “As a result, several necessary measures under the malaria programme were not taken,” one official said.

“Until the outbreak began, on paper the malaria situation looked under control,” the official said.

Mosquito nets were not distributed by the government this year in four villages that Scroll visited. In several villages, spraying and fogging insecticides to kill mosquitoes was delayed.

Sunder Markam, a contractual worker, said he was appointed to conduct fogging in affected villages from August 12 after a jump in malaria cases.

In Kundekasa village, where four-year-old Arvind Dhurwey died of malaria, sarpanch Parshuram Dhurwey said the health department did not undertake any preventive measures to control the mosquito spread till July end. “All these fogging teams have come after the deaths began to increase,” he said.

Experts say one more factor explains the fatalities in the area – malnutrition.

When the measles outbreak hit villages here, along with a sharp rise in malaria infections, malnourished children got seriously ill. Many caught both diseases.

Of the 150 children admitted in a primary health centre in Bithli village in Balaghat since July, medical officer Dr Saurabh Uikey counted over 50 as underweight. “Malnourishment makes recovery difficult,” he said. “Children are susceptible to even the smallest of infections and can die of preventable diseases.”

Virologist Shahid Jameel agreed. He told Scroll that malaria can “weaken the immunity system” and malnourishment can “compound the severity of the underlying health conditions”.

Every third child aged under five is underweight in Balaghat, data from the National Family Health Survey-6 shows.

But the data recorded by Balaghat’s Women and Child Development department officials appeared to be seriously undercounting the levels of malnourishment, Scroll found on the ground.

For example, in three anganwadis we visited, only five of 127 children were recorded as severely acute malnourished children – that is one in every 25 children. There was no record of moderate acute malnourished children even though several children were shockingly underweight.

Professor Vijay Nema, from the National Institute for Tribal Health Research, who visited Balaghat to investigate the outbreak, said that they found severely malnourished children during their field visits. “We do not need to measure their arm circumference to know that. They clearly looked undernourished,” he said.

He added: “A vaccine may not fully work on severely malnourished children.”

In Bondari village, three-year-old Priyanka Dhurwey had been vaccinated against measles, her father Sukhchand said.

She was one of the few children who had reached a hospital facility after falling sick with suspected measles symptoms.

But Priyanka died within two days of hospitalisation. In official records, her cause of death is “severe acute malnutrition, severe respiratory distress, severe anaemia, shock and respiratory failure”.

When Priyanka died on August 13, she weighed 4 kg. “That’s the weight of a two-month old baby,” said Rajaram Chandrawanshi, district early intervention officer. A child her age should ideally weigh between 11 kg and 15 kg.

Priyanka was not even listed as a malnourished child in the anganwadi’s register.

According to anganwadi workers in the villages, children’s nutrition was adversely affected recently when the government has stopped supplying take-home rations. Until March, children aged three or less received free food from the state government’s Women and Child Development department. The take-home-rations – rice, dal, soybean – were given to maintain a basic nutritional diet in children.The aid stopped five months ago after the Madhya Pradesh government failed to pay the agencies supplying the food.

“The last supply came in March. That stock lasted till April,” said Kundekasa’s anganwadi worker Mamta Yadav.

Sukhchand, Priyanka’s father, said in the last few months, after the rations stopped, “she had become very weak”.

“Anganwadi food helps many poor families in this region. We have been telling our supervisors to make some alternative arrangements,” said Suhadra Yadav, an anganwadi worker in Matla village.

Devendra Sundriyal, assistant director in the women and child development department, did not respond to Scroll’s calls and texts, asking about take-home rations not being delivered and the poor record-keeping at the anganwadi.

Local residents claim that malnourishment is a failure of multiple government departments, not just the Women and Child Development.

Mansaram Meravi, member of the local Zilla Parishad, said several tribal residents have not been able to avail forest resources and land rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, which affected their traditional source of nutrition.

The Baiga tribe traditionally relies on forest produce – they gather elephant foot yam, pihri or edible mushroom, and tubers from the forest to cook and eat. “Several are not allowed to gather forest produce,” said Meravi. “Their movement in the forest is now heavily controlled by the government.”

editorials.title: How Ahmedabad became an unwelcoming city
editorials.passage:
In 1972, community organiser Ela Bhatt and a group of women met at Ahmedabad’s Victoria Garden to discuss the conditions in which self-employed women worked. That meeting led to the formation of the Self-Employed Women’s Association, or SEWA, which became one of India’s most significant labour organisations.

Ahmedabad’s public spaces have never just been places to pass the time: since the freedom struggle, they have hosted many important gatherings meant to organise, debate and build political movements.

That history makes the attack on a reading gathering at AUDA Garden in Vastrapur on August 27 particularly revealing. A group of people had gathered to read books including Anne Frank’s diary, Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala , Bhagat Singh’s Why I Am an Atheist and George Orwell’s 1984 . Members of the Bajrang Dal disrupted the gathering and assaulted some of those present.

The organisation later said its objection was directed at Yousafzai, citing her views on Pakistan and Kashmir. The incident followed a controversy at a school in the city, where members of the Bajrang Dal and Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad – Hindutva groups under the umbrella of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh – objected to the inclusion of I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s diary in the school’s reading programme.

The school eventually made the books optional and ended the contract of the consultant who had been involved in developing its curriculum.

Hindutva supporters have presented the argument about the books as though this were a dispute over curriculum. That isn’t particularly convincing. The school has said that the books were part of an optional book club rather than the compulsory curriculum. Yet, a reading list containing two internationally recognised books became a political controversy, and the response to protest outside the school and pressure the institution until it changed its position instead of examining the books through an educational process.

More revealingly, the objection reported by The Times of India was that the books were associated with people of “other religions”. The books were turned into proxies for their authors’ identities and the school was pressured to treat those identities as a legitimate reason to restrict what children could read. Those objecting to these books were identifying a Muslim author and a Jewish author as politically suspect and then using (dis)organised pressure to determine whether children should encounter their work.

This was not the first instance of an educational institution in Ahmedabad being confronted by political muscle.

In 2018, historian Ramachandra Guha was appointed at Ahmedabad University and was expected to direct its Gandhi Winter School. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, the student wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, protested almost immediately, threatening violence. Guha, noted for his scholarship on Gandhi, eventually did not join the university.

In March 2020, at IIM Ahmedabad, a doctoral thesis on electoral democracy attracted the attention of Bharatiya Janata Party politician Subramanian Swamy because it explored how the Hindutva organisation mobilises around caste and religion. Swamy took to X to target the young scholar, a woman, and her advisor (who was then the director of the institute). Both were harassed and subjected to vitriol for months after that.

In April 2020, the Union education ministry subsequently asked IIM Ahmedabad for a copy of the thesis but the institute denied the request. Again, political actors considered themselves entitled to intervene in what was being produced and circulated as academic research.

At Gujarat University in 2024, outstation students were attacked in their hostel after a group objected to them offering namaz during Ramzan. Students were injured, rooms and vehicles were vandalised, and the incident resulted in criminal cases.

These incidents are a part of a history of political and religious organisations claiming the authority to decide what is acceptable in Ahmedabad’s schools, universities and public spaces.

In April 2002, shortly after the Gujarat riots, a peace meeting at Gandhi’s Sabarmati Ashram was attacked by a mob protesting the presence of activist Medha Patkar, whose Narmada Bachao Andolan had opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam that is one of the state’s signature projects. Patkar was surrounded and threatened, journalists covering the meeting were assaulted, and participants were manhandled.

News reports described police as initially standing by before eventually intervening. The irony of a peace meeting being attacked inside Gandhi's ashram was not lost on anyone, but the incident was significant for another reason: the people holding the meeting had chosen the Ashram because threats had already forced them to abandon another venue.

Ahmedabad has never had a straightforward relationship with the idea of a common public.

The Sabarmati Riverfront is a clear example of this pattern. Its development in 2012 was framed as the reclamation and beautification of public space, but the project displaced thousands of people who had lived and worked along the river. Research on the completed riverfront has also found that parts of this new public space are privately managed, with guards preventing street vendors and squatters from using the promenades.

Ahmedabad’s parks are part of this same dynamic. The city now has hundreds of municipal parks and gardens, but public space is about more than whether everyone is allowed in. It is also about whether a group of young people can gather there, whether someone can pray there, whether people can hold a political discussion, whether a Muslim woman can sit there without becoming conspicuous and whether a group can read books that someone else considers politically offensive without being confronted by a mob.

The Disturbed Areas Act is a more formal expression of this anxiety. Introduced in Gujarat in 1991 in the aftermath of communal violence, the law was intended to prevent distress sales and protect people from being forced out of areas affected by communal tensions.

However, over time, it has reinforced religious segregation in Ahmedabad by restricting certain property transfers between members of different communities. What began as a protective measure has become part of the machinery by which the city’s communal geography is maintained.

There is extensive research on how this segregation affects access to housing, public space and everyday mobility. If a neighbourhood has become religiously segregated through decades of violence, fear and displacement, then preventing people from changing that demographic composition can be justified as necessary to preserve communal harmony. Segregation creates the condition to justify maintaining segregation.

The Gujarat government expanded this framework in 2026, changing the terminology from “disturbed areas” to “specified areas”, giving authorities wider powers over property transactions.

Earlier this year, the Gujarat High Court struck down an order preventing a Hindu-owned property in Jamalpur from being sold to the Muslim family that had rented it for decades. One of the concerns about the transaction had been its potential effect on the religious composition of the area. The court rejected the idea that demographic change could simply be treated as sufficient reason to block a property transaction.

The connection between the Disturbed Areas Act and the mob in the Vastrapur park is not direct. One relates to who can buy property in a neighbourhood. The other relates to what people can do in a park. But both become easier to understand in a city where communal identity has already been allowed to determine so much of the physical and social landscape.

There is an irony in this happening in Ahmedabad, a city with such a strong history of political organising and public debate. The women who met in Victoria Garden in 1972 were using the public space available to them to organise around their own interests. That is what public space is supposed to make possible: people who do not necessarily have institutional power finding each other, talking, reading, organising.

Now, the question is about what kind of public life Ahmedabad is willing to permit.

Saachi D’Souza is a writer and editor from Goa, working on reportage, essays and fiction on culture, identity, and politics.

editorials.title: War history: How India fought against Pakistan’s military attack in the Rann of Kutch in 1965
editorials.passage:
Since Partition in August 1947, Pakistan had laid claim to the northern half of the Great Rann of Kutch, up to the line of 24 degrees north latitude, covering an area of more than 9,000 square kilometres, on the following grounds.

The first argument was that the Rann of Kutch could either be considered a landlocked sea or a boundary lake, and therefore the international boundary should run through the middle.

The second argument was that the northern half of the Rann had been administered by Sindh since its annexation by the British in 1843. Several pre- and post-Partition documents were cited in support of this claim.

Pakistan launched Operation Desert Hawk I in January 1965. The aim of this operation was fourfold.

To assess the Indian response and evaluate its defences.

To draw the Indian Army away from Punjab to Kutch.

To give Pakistani forces a dress rehearsal for a full-scale invasion of India later in the year, first in Jammu and Kashmir and later in Punjab.

To ascertain how serious the United States was in enforcing its ban on the use of American-supplied military hardware against India.

In early April 1965, the Pakistan Army made a bid to capture a small post southwest of Kanjarkot called Sardar Post and another further to the southeast called Vigokot. The aim of these attacks was to overrun Indian positions right up to the 24th parallel north latitude. These attempts were beaten back by the Indian Army, which had rushed reinforcements to the area. Pakistan now prepared to launch Operation Desert Hawk II. During this phase, extensive exchanges of fire took place between patrols of the two sides, but the fighting was largely confined to the areas around Sardar Post and Vigokot.

At this time, a very unusual event occurred. The chief of the air staff of the Pakistan Air Force, Air Marshal Asghar Khan, called his Indian counterpart, Air Marshal Arjan Singh, and suggested that both sides should refrain from using offensive aircraft such as fighters and bombers in the Kutch area until the issue was resolved amicably. Air Marshal Arjan Singh remained non-committal and stated that he would have to keep the government of India informed.

On April 25, 1965, Pakistan launched a brigade-sized attack supported by thirty tanks on Biar Bet, which lay 38 kilometres to the west of Chhad Bet. After heavy fighting, the Indian Army withdrew from Biar Bet. Thereafter, further action was restricted to patrolling by both sides and sporadic shelling.

On April 26, 1965, Defence Minister YB Chavan announced in Parliament that the Indian Armed Forces had been placed on alert following general mobilisation in Pakistan. The Indian Air Force reinforced pilot strength in front-line squadrons by recalling experienced pilots serving on instructional duties in Training Command and attaching them to operational squadrons in aircraft on which they were already qualified. Normal training flying in operational squadrons was curtailed in order to conserve flying hours.

The defence minister’s statement in Parliament triggered an international response. British Prime Minister Harold Wilson wrote to both Lal Bahadur Shastri and President Ayub Khan suggesting a ceasefire. He proposed a return to status quo ante as it existed on January 1, 1965. However, the definition of status quo ante itself became contentious, as both sides wanted their respective positions incorporated in any agreement. It was eventually agreed to cease all hostile actions from May 1, 1965 while talks were in progress.

India was looking for hard evidence of the use of American-supplied equipment, especially Patton tanks, during the border skirmishes. No. 101 Fighter Reconnaissance Squadron was at Armament Training Wing, Jamnagar, undergoing its annual armament training. The squadron was equipped with Vampire T.55 trainer aircraft fitted with three F.95 cameras mounted in the bulbous nose, one looking forward and one on either side looking sideways.

On April 26, 1965, under orders from Air Headquarters, an early morning fighter reconnaissance sortie was launched to collect photographic evidence of the use of American-supplied Patton tanks during the incursion. The Vampire T.55 was captained by Flying Officer Utpal Barbara with Flying Officer JP Chhetri as his co-pilot. A single-seater Vampire FB.52 was sent as a fighter escort.

Barbara was able to locate the target area in spite of poor visibility caused by dust haze. He spotted deep tracks in the sandy soil well inside Indian territory. He correctly assessed that these were made by tracked vehicles, possibly tanks, and began filming. A short distance ahead he came across a tank column and made several photo runs over it at about 100 feet above ground level to obtain close-up shots.

During the mission, he encountered flak and small-arms fire. Undeterred, he made repeated passes to collect irrefutable evidence of the use of American-supplied equipment. Fortunately, his aircraft was not hit.

After about five minutes over the area of incursion, the formation returned safely to base. The films were developed quickly and, a couple of hours later, Barbara carrying a packet of valuable photographs, took off for Delhi in a Vampire FB.65. On landing at Palam airport, he was picked up in a staff car and driven to Army Headquarters, where he personally briefed the chief of the army staff. Army Headquarters confirmed that the photographs showed Patton tanks and that Pakistani involvement was exposed. Flying Officer Utpal Barbara was awarded a well-deserved Vir Chakra for his gallant action.

On June 17, 1965, Prime Minister Shastri and President Ayub Khan met at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers’ Conference in London and agreed to a ceasefire. A formal ceasefire was announced by both sides on June 29, 1965.

Pakistan had initiated the Kutch border skirmishes to test Indian political resolve to counter aggression along its borders. The Pakistani establishment concluded, incorrectly, that Indian resolve was weak. In addition, Pakistan assessed that the October and November 1962 conflict with China had militarily weakened India. Pakistan was now emboldened to attempt annexation of Jammu and Kashmir by military means.

Excerpted with permission from The Sabre Slayers: The Air Battles of the 1965 War with Pakistan, Philip Rajkumar and Shiv Kunal Verma, Aleph Book Company.

editorials.title: Salman Rushdie strikes again — this time in ‘Silly-man’ style
editorials.passage:
Sir Salman got his surname from the Arabic word Rushdi, meaning “mature” or “wise”. His life, however, suggests that this otherwise brilliant novelist has often been anything but mature or wise. And now, he can be accused of being economical with the truth — or, worse, of peddling falsehoods and distortions.

There he was, in an interview recently, being asked about the RSS chief’s recent visit to New York. The framing of the questions was disturbingly biased. The anchor began by describing the RSS as “a Hindu nationalist organisation” that has been “described as a far-right paramilitary organisation accused of committing human rights violations”.

A far-right paramilitary organisation? Really?

But Salman Rushdie, far from being perturbed by this description, went on to add a sweeping comparison of his own: “It is unfortunately the case that a lot of Indian Americans” — here he paused to add — “Hindu Americans are attracted to the idea of Hindu nationalism. You can compare it, if you want, to the way in which Irish Americans used to support the IRA.”

The comparison is extraordinarily reckless. The Irish Republican Army, during the Troubles (from the late 1960s to 1998), carried out thousands of armed actions, shootings and bombings. In 1972 alone, the Provisional IRA reportedly carried out more than a thousand bomb attacks. Over three decades, London was repeatedly targeted with explosives. Encyclopaedia Britannica estimates that the Provisional IRA killed about 1,800 people between 1969 and 1994, including about 600 civilians.

To equate support for the RSS among Hindu Americans with Irish-American support for the IRA is therefore an extremely irresponsible comparison. But Rushdie’s distortions did not stop there. When asked whether the “secular India” in which he “grew up in a secular Muslim family” was gone forever, he replied: “Forever is a long time.”

So, “is secular India retrievable”?

Sir Salman responded: “I am very impressed by young people in India. Enormously impressed by the women who are refusing the kind of limitations on the way women are supposed to behave.”

It is a suitably progressive-sounding response, but it sidesteps truth, again. Large numbers of young Indians, including women, have repeatedly voted for the BJP since 2014. Perhaps Rushdie’s view of contemporary Bharat is increasingly shaped by the ‘secular’, ‘liberal’ and elitist circles in which he now lives.

Rushdie then accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of being “in part responsible” for the 2002 post-Godhra Gujarat violence. Even more disturbing was the disdain he appeared to show for the country’s democratic and legal institutions. He said: “Many of us suspect that the leadership of Gujarat, one of the big states of India — and he was the chief minister — that the Hindu leadership of the state was involved in encouraging what became a murderous moment in the life of the state. I mean, look, we have to say that he was exonerated, but what does that mean, and who did the exoneration?”

Sir Salman, India’s highest court has dealt with allegations concerning Modi’s role in the Gujarat violence. One is entitled to question a political leader, of course. But casually casting doubt on the legitimacy of judicial findings merely because they do not conform to one’s suspicions is a different matter altogether. But then, that is Rushdie for you. Over the years, particularly since his years in hiding following the Iranian fatwa, he appears to have become increasingly selective in his application of truth and liberalism.

He readily calls out fundamentalism, but his rhetoric can seem markedly sharper when directed at what he regards as Hindutva than when confronting Islamism. Perhaps experience has taught him caution. Calling out Islamist extremism can carry terrible consequences; Rushdie himself knows that better than almost anyone alive. Attacking Hindutva, by comparison, carries a very different kind of risk in the Western intellectual circles he inhabits.

Maybe this writer is being too scathing about Rushdie. After all, he seems to be merely following a familiar ‘liberal’ playbook. Consider Gopalkrishna Gandhi’s article in an Indian daily in August 2022, shortly after Rushdie was stabbed in New York. While examining the Rushdie stabbing, Gandhi seemed oblivious to the attacker’s identity — the writer didn’t mention even once why the novelist was attacked, who the attacker was, or why Rushdie was forced to stay under cover for years despite issuing several apologies. Instead, he invoked Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination by a Hindu in 1948. His verdict became intriguingly problematic when he wrote, “The attack on Rushdie comes from the same source?”

Rushdie’s latest warning about the RSS and “Hindu nationalism” appears to follow a similar Left-‘liberal’ pattern: first, minimise or qualify the ideological dimensions of Islamist violence; then, when the violence becomes impossible to ignore, search for an equivalent within Hindu nationalism. So much so that it has now begun to look less like a principled intellectual position and more like the behaviour of a man barking up the one tree that never bit him, while carefully avoiding the forest of blades that cost him an eye and left him grievously wounded. Perhaps Rushdie understands better than most the consequences of taking on a real ideological bully. The temptation, then, is obvious: retain the moral high ground by confronting the safer adversary. This way he retains his ‘progressive’ halo without inviting any fatal injury to himself.

It’s like a traumatised person avoiding the bully while lecturing those from whom he expects no comparable retaliation. Writers like Ayaan Hirsi Ali have described this phenomenon as the “fear-shaped silence” that hangs over critiques of Islamism. Rushdie may not be totally silent, but he is certainly cautious, careful to look for the safer target while framing his criticisms of Islamism within layers of diplomatic phrasing. He is well aware, better than anyone else, of the one ideology that puts a global contract on life that never gets revoked.

In his memoir Joseph Anton, Rushdie recalls the moment in 1989 when Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued the fatwa against him. A BBC reporter telephoned and asked how it felt to know that he had just been sentenced to death. It was a sunny Tuesday in London, but Rushdie had never felt the world so dark. “It doesn’t feel good,” he replied, though inwardly he thought, “I’m a dead man.”

Perhaps a part of Salman Rushdie did die that day. Maybe the rebel part. As the saying goes, you either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain. Sadly, Rushdie, the rebel, has lived long enough to become a sort of Left-‘liberal’ clown. And he has done it again — in a “Silly-man” style.

(Utpal Kumar is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: What is Prince Harry really bothered about after ‘ghar wapsi’?
editorials.passage:
Politics makes strange bedfellows, goes the proverb born out of the vagaries of powerplay in Britain in the past few centuries. But of late, democracy and the importance of public opinion there has led to equally strange happenings in the House of Windsor, judging from the emanations from its outposts in Clarence House (where King Charles and Queen Camilla actually live) and Buckingham Palace, where their offices, staff and courtiers are stationed.

This week ‘the Palace’ — in this case the Lord Chamberlain — issued a ‘guidance’ that the newly-returned Prince Harry and his American duchess are to be regarded as “private citizens”, not “working royals”. This was apparently in response to queries from many quarters on how the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are to be greeted and treated when they carry out engagements in the UK. Such concerns are expected, after all Harry is a son of the reigning monarch.

The Palace has basically clarified that Harry and Meghan’s engagements are not to be deemed ‘royal’ events — which necessitate bows and curtseys. The Sussexes are also not to use HRH (His/Her Royal Highness) prefixes — that mandates bows and curtseys — as those are still “held in abeyance”. While the couple clearly smarted at that ponderously worded rebuke, the minutae of royal protocol may not be known to everyone or indeed deemed important by anyone.

Royalty worldwide all profess to be “modern” now and try to give the impression that they are “normal” people. But there is a difference between modernity and equality and those little details like prefixes and protocols set them apart from the aam janta and reiterate (to themselves, mostly) their “bluebloodedness” in an era of fast-spreading republicanism. Even now, some of India’s de-royalised ‘princes’ still want to be addressed as ‘his/her highness’, at least privately.

When 13-year-old Prince George, flanked by his parents the Prince and Princess of Wales, arrived at Eton College for his first day earlier this week, the Provost Sir Nicholas Coleridge bowed (now basically from the neck rather than the waist) to all three. Prince George and his parents also greet his grandfather King Charles and step-grandmother Queen Camilla with bow and curtsy respectively, as do the two younger Wales children, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.

Indeed, bobbing rows of Windsors of all ages each time the monarch walks by them is a commonly seen phenomenon and bespeaks their devotion to ancient royal decorum. No wonder there has been considerable gleeful media speculation about whether the disgraced and de-royalised Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, bows to his daughters, who are still styled as princesses. Prince Harry’s anxiety about where he stands in this bobbing order is very understandable.

After all, to make a success of his return to the UK, Harry has to regain his lost royal lustre; being a private citizen rather than a public prince will not suit him. But the fact that Buckingham Palace responded at all to queries paradoxically underlines his continuing membership of the British Royal Family. Harry has not become Henry Mountbatten Windsor, Esq. and what he does in the UK cannot be seen separately from his identity as the younger son of the King.

The general public will also see the pathos in Harry’s situation. He is back in the country whose monarch he calls Pa. The previous monarch, Queen Elizabeth II was Granny. Both, by birthright. And yet here he is “a Prince of the blood royal” being put in his place by “a man in a grey suit”—as Harry has famously described courtiers, which would per se include the Lord Chamberlain. Unless he protests and protects his inherent “princeliness” it could be detrimental.

His fight with the establishment for official security for himself and his family also seems to be linked to that assertion of royalty. There is no threat to their lives; any assault would be on their privacy. By royal convention Prince George will not be hounded by the British media while at Eton though that may not save him from phone cameras. By asserting Harry is a non-working royal the palace seems to be throwing the Sussexes under the media and social media bus.

The Palace announcement also sounds churlish. After all, when mere commoners are treated like royalty because they happen to be celebrities, why should some royals be treated like commoners because they happen to be celebrities? Red carpets and band-baaja, bowing and scraping are standard protocol at every gala event. But will the palace diktat on “private citizens” make organisers chary of extending this basic royal-style bandobast to the poor Sussexes?

It seems as though the Palace is too sensitive to possible social media opprobrium. Are they so spooked by their own slow reaction to the public mood back when Princess Diana died in 1997 that they now want to get in front of any possible blowback on Harry and Meghan? They appear to be second guessing the public reaction based on umpteen opinion polls and media prognostications rather than looking at the Sussex ghar wapsi issue dispassionately and sensibly.

Amid this royal kerfuffle over bandobast, the question that remains unanswered is why the Sussexes decided to return to the UK at all, six years after they left in high dudgeon and later lobbed several incendiary devices at their royal relatives. Was it to recharge their royal batteries before returning for a second US innings? Was it because Meghan wanted the children to have some relationship with their grandfather, with future prospects in mind? Was Harry homesick?

On that answer would depend the cost-benefit analysis of their return. Is it worth the humiliation of Palace diktats about their status? Is it worth the pain of possibly being left out of seasonal Royal Family gatherings despite blood relationships? The effect of all this on how Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet regard their Wales first cousins, one of whom will be king some day, cannot be ignored either. How the Wales children regard their Sussex cousins is also germane.

Too much water has flowed down the Thames to expect a speedy, right royal reconciliation between the Sussexes and the King and Queen and the Waleses, although they are all the same family at the end of the day. But even blueblood is thicker than water, so an eventual royal rapprochement cannot be deemed entirely off the table. Much will depend on how both camps react to any future provocation and media hype of any “differences”, imagined or real.

(The author is a freelance writer. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely that of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: A Veteran at Ram Mandir's Helm: Why the Uniform Must Stay Above Politics
editorials.passage: There is nothing inherently controversial about appointing a military veteran to administer a major public institution. Quite the contrary. Veterans are among the country's most under-utilised repositories of institutional capability. Decades of service teach them something increasingly rare in public life, i.e., discipline without drama, accountability without evasion, hierarchy without personal aggrandisement, and the ability to take decisions under pressure.A distinguished military officer carries with them more than a résumé. He/she carries institutionalised experience, administrative rigour, constitutional bearing and, ideally, a deeply ingrained sense of service to the nation. When such experience is deployed in civilian institutions where it is genuinely needed, society benefits.That is why the appointment of Air Marshal (retd) Jeetendra Mishra as the first full-time CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust should not be criticised merely because he is a veteran. The veteran is not the problem. Indeed, his professional experience may prove precisely what an institution undergoing administrative scrutiny requires.But precisely because the appointment is consequential, it deserves scrutiny of a different kind. The question is not whether a decorated Air Marshal is competent. The question is what symbolic and political work his presence may inadvertently perform. The uniform is larger than the person.How Jeetendra Mishra Beat 5,585 Applicants to Become Ram Mandir Trust CEOThe Indian military uniform occupies a singular place in our national imagination. It is proudly secular. It is constitutionally anchored. It belongs to no party, no ideology, no caste and no religion. A soldier does not defend a Hindu India, a Muslim India, a Sikh India or a Christian India. He/she serves India. That distinction is not semantic. It is foundational. The extraordinary legitimacy enjoyed by the uniform derives precisely from its distance from partisan and sectarian identity. The armed forces are one of the few institutions in public life where the constitutional promise of equality is not merely an aspiration but an operational necessity.Which is why there is a subliminal danger when the enormous moral capital of the uniform is transported into a religiously and politically charged institution. The danger is not that the veteran suddenly becomes less secular. The danger is that religiosity may begin to attach itself, however subliminally, to the symbolism of the secular uniform. That is a line worth guarding carefully.To pretend that the Ram Mandir is entirely bereft of political angularity would itself be naive. The temple is an enormously consequential religious institution, but its construction and public meaning are inseparable from one of the most politically transformative movements in contemporary India. That reality need not diminish the religious significance of the temple. It simply means that anyone administering it operates within a landscape that is simultaneously religious, social and political.Into that landscape now comes a former Air Marshal. The optics, therefore, matter. A decorated military officer at the helm of the Ram Mandir may, entirely unintentionally, create an association between two sources of extraordinary public reverence ie, the sanctity of the temple and the sanctity of the uniform.That association is precisely what a secular republic should be cautious about manufacturing. The armed forces should remain above religious proprietorship. Their institutional identity must never acquire a denominational hue by association, however innocent or administratively motivated. The uniform belongs to the Constitution. It does not belong to a temple, mosque, church, or a gurudwara. Then there is another, more uncomfortable dimension. Politicians understand the power of institutional credibility. They also understand that placing an individual of unquestioned personal stature into a controversial or politically sensitive institution can alter the terms of public scrutiny. This is where the veteran can become something he never intended to be—political “cover fire”.The point is not to allege that the former Air Marshal has been appointed for that purpose. There is no basis for imputing such a motive to him. The point is that political actors can benefit from the optics, regardless of the appointee's intentions.When a veteran with an illustrious career is placed in a position of authority, criticism can become psychologically more difficult. Questions about administrative failure can acquire an unnecessary halo of patriotism. Questions about institutional responsibility can become entangled with respect for military service. And allegations that ought to be answered institutionally may instead be deflected by the credibility of the person occupying the chair. That is an unhealthy inversion.A veteran's reputation should strengthen accountability, not substitute for it. Indeed, this is particularly relevant when the institution has been under scrutiny over allegations concerning donation management and administrative lapses. The appropriate response to such controversy is not merely to put a highly credible individual at the top. It is to build systems that make credibility irrelevant to accountability. No institution should require the public to trust a person's résumé in order to trust its accounts.Naravane Memoir Row: Risks of Militarising Politics & Politicising the SoldierThere is also a broader principle here that deserves to be defended without embarrassment. India's secularism does not require the state or its institutions to be hostile to religion. It requires constitutional institutions to resist being captured by religious identity. The military's secularism is particularly precious because it represents India at its most elemental - citizens of different faiths standing in the same uniform under the same flag.That uniform should, therefore, be deployed in civilian life with some sensitivity to the symbolic terrain into which it is being placed.There is nothing wrong with a veteran serving a religious institution. Veterans are citizens, and they have every right to serve wherever their abilities are useful. But the distinction between the veteran as an individual citizen and the uniform as a national institution must remain unmistakable.The distinguished former Air Marshal has every right to take up a civilian role. The country has every right to insist that his military legacy is not appropriated to sanctify the institution, its politics or its administration. And the government has a responsibility to ensure that it is not.Veterans deserve better than tokenism and politicians deserve scrutiny. This is ultimately an argument for veterans, not against them. If governments genuinely believe that military veterans possess extraordinary administrative capability, then India should systematically employ them in public administration, infrastructure, disaster management, public-sector reform and institutional governance.But they should be appointed for competence, given genuine operational autonomy and judged by measurable outcomes. They should not be used as human credibility certificates. A former military commander should never become the answer to a question that remains unanswered.If the Ram Mandir requires professionalisation, professionalise it. If its finances require greater transparency, provide it. If its donation systems require reform, reform them. If responsibility for past administrative lapses needs to be established, establish it. And if political interference is a problem, insulate the institution from it. Do all of this under the stewardship of a veteran if his expertise makes him the best person for the job.But do not allow his uniform to become either a religious symbol or a political shield. That would be a disservice to the very institution from which he comes. The Indian military uniform is powerful precisely because it transcends the divisions of Indian society. It represents a constitutional India in which the soldier's faith is private but his oath is public; his identity may be particular, but his allegiance is indivisible.That distinction must survive every civilian appointment. The Ram Mandir deserves competent administration. The public deserves accountability. Veterans deserve to be valued for their capability rather than appropriated for their credibility. And the uniform deserves something even more important ie, to remain above the politics of the temple, just as it remains above the politics of the ballot box.(Bhopinder Singh is the former Lieutenant Governor of The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry.
